## 231. A second citation reader that never uses blame, and what its first measurement said (D228)

The forward correction owed by the previous unit, filed here rather than amended: that unit's closing sentence
described the pre-landing census (four cites unjudged because their writer was the all-zero sha) while the
reading taken after its own commit was one unjudged and one hundred twenty-nine exact. Both numbers were true,
of different planes, and the sentence named neither. It is corrected by stating the plane every time from now on.

Then the durable thing this unit built: a reader that asks a different question of the same citations, because
the question the drift reader asks cannot be asked of a re-aim. It takes the tokens a ledger sentence puts in
backticks next to a citation, calls them the referent, and asks whether the cited line holds one of them. No
blame, no writer commit, no self-credit: the commit that lands a wrong re-aim is judged on the same terms as a
year-old one. It also reads both ends of a range and every continuation, which is the endpoint the other reader
never prints.

Measured on the committed plane, over the two ledgers: five hundred forty-five citation endpoints, of which three
hundred seventy name a file through a path this reader will not resolve · a bare basename, or a package path the
repository spells elsewhere · the same class the shipped reader declines, ninety-eight sit in lines whose
neighbours carry no code token, one is past EOF, and
seventy-six are judged. Of those: sixteen land on the referent's line, eleven within three lines, forty-nine do
not, zero are absent from the file entirely.

The forty-nine are not forty-nine findings, and the run says why: the token grammar accepts words that are not
code · the last step of the range check turned on the token 'this' · and a citation that names a block rather
than a line reads as a miss by construction. So this reader is a scratch instrument and not a gate step, and the
judged population is far below the drift reader's because being strict about tokens costs population.

Where it did earn its keep is the pair of known answers. The range repaired by the last unit reads stale at the
old plane on BOTH endpoints and matched at the new plane on the start; that is a citation reader whose verdict
moves with the number instead of with the commit. The other repaired pair reads matched at both planes, which is
a blind spot: those lines hold nothing but the path, so the reader has no referent to test and passes either
way. It is recorded as a limit, not fixed by loosening the token rule.

One new finding, named and deliberately not repaired. The sentence that cites the workflow range claims three
steps pipe a checker into tee. At the committed plane the file holds ten tee commands · thirteen lines mention
the word, three of them the comment that introduced the region · and nine of the commands sit inside that region.
So either the count in the sentence is stale or the range does not cover the
steps the sentence means; deciding which needs the original finding re-read, and rewriting a number without
reading it is the mistake this lane has now paid for twice. Open on purpose.

Readings on this plane: the drift census unchanged at one hundred twenty-nine exact of one hundred forty-seven
judged, zero moved, zero non-unique; nothing in the ledgers edited in place; the gate untouched; nothing pushed.
## 232. The finding the last unit left open was mine, and reading the defining commit falsified it (D229)

The open item was stated as a count conflict: a ledger sentence cites a workflow range and claims three piped
steps, while the committed workflow supposedly holds ten of them. It was written down without reading the sentence
twice, and reading it kills the finding. The three is a claim about the moment of the original defect; the same
paragraph quotes the current census as its own derived number, seven, so the file already distinguishes the two
tenses. My ten came from counting every line that mentions the word, three of which are the comment that introduces
the region, and from treating a checker-piping step and a step writing to the job output as one population.
Retracted, and the retraction is the point: a number I typed from a grep is a claim about my grep.

What reading the commit that made the claim did find is worse than a stale count, and it is mine. The commit that
introduced the shell note piped exactly three pre-existing checkers into the artifact writer, and at the committed
plane those three steps run from line two hundred fifteen to line two hundred thirty-six. The ledger's range said
two twenty-four to two fifty-four · four piped steps, the last two of which belong to readers written long after
that finding. And the two twenty-four start was not inherited drift: it is where THIS lane's previous unit moved
the number, replacing a two fifteen that was right. The referent auditor reported that repair as matched on its
start, which is the self-credit property arriving by a new route · a re-aim can be certified by a reader that only
asks whether the new line holds a token, because matching the wrong line is a true statement about the wrong thing.

A second site fell to the same method. An early section cites the workflow's contract-drift step at line two hundred
two; that line is inside the comment block, and the step that runs the checker in report mode is two eighteen. The
drift reader has never objected, because a citation into comment prose moves with the file it names, which is exactly
the exemption its own header warns a gate cannot carry.

Both repairs went through an applier that reads the committed text, requires the pattern to occur once, requires it
to occur on the predicted line, and writes nothing if any row refuses; two rows, two single matches, two lines
rewritten, no other byte touched.

Readings on this plane, after the edits: the drift census still judges one hundred forty-seven citations, but the two
touched sites are now reached rather than judged · while the edit is uncommitted their writer is the all-zero sha · so
exact one hundred twenty-eight, gone one hundred sixteen, no-base three, and one of those three is the re-aim that took
a gone row out of the queue. On the landing commit both sites read judged by construction, the self-credit property
again, which is why the clearing is claimed from the target file and not from the census. The strict pass exits 0; the
comment-plane reader reports zero strict offenders; the section reader and the section-citation reader both pass; the
referent auditor keeps publishing its own false-positive count as the reason it is still a scratch instrument.
## 233. A reader that decides a citation by the SURFACE of the line it names, and the three bugs that hid before it judged anything (D230)

The rule is mechanical on both sides. The cited line gets a surface class in the target file at the ref being
judged: nothing there is blank, a line whose first non-space token is that language's comment marker is a comment,
a line that declares something nameable is a declaration, anything else is code. The citing text gets a claim verb
from a closed list, taken from the CITATION'S OWN CLAUSE · the span around it between the nearest boundary
characters that lie outside code spans and outside any citation. A sentence that says a line runs a checker while
pointing at a comment is then a contradiction nobody has to interpret. Paragraph joining is part of the rule
rather than a nicety: the ledger wraps near one hundred twenty columns, so a line is a fragment of a sentence, and
the first version of this reader paired verbs with citations per line.

That first version reddened two sentences that are correct, which is how the wrapping bug showed up. One cites the
workflow's explanatory note: the sentence reads that all three steps declare a shell now, under a note that says
why, and the citation names the note. The verb belongs to the steps; the citation's own clause already declares its
surface to be a note, and the line it points at is that note. The other matched the word run out of the phrase
"comment run" · a noun, two clauses further along, in a sentence that claims nothing about the cited block. Both
rows were refusals of text that agrees with the files.

Clause scoping then needed two masking fixes of its own, each of which was a false red before it was fixed.
Code spans cannot be paired across the joined paragraph: one line with an unclosed backtick makes a paragraph-wide
toggle mask every boundary character to the end, and the clause then re-absorbs the very cross-clause verbs the
scoping exists to exclude · that artifact alone produced a third refusal on a correct row. And the walk leftward
from a citation must start at the path, not at the character the citation regex consumed before it, because that
character is frequently the opening parenthesis that bounds a parenthesised reference.

Sensitivity was checked against the site this class came from, and it survives. The early section that says the
workflow's report-mode step runs a checker, pointing inside the explanatory comment, is refused at the plane before
the repair and reads matched at the repaired plane; the same workflow file is byte-identical across those two
refs, so the only variable is the ledger's own text. The refusal set on that older plane went from three rows to
one, and the one left is the real defect.

What stops this becoming a gate step is a number the reader prints about itself. With clause scoping, six citation
sites carry a claim verb inside their own clause while one hundred twenty-one have a verb somewhere in the
paragraph and none in the clause. The gap is not the scoping: it is the closed verb list, which misses the verbs
this ledger actually uses to make a claim about a line · gates, records, marks, tells, keeps, stamps, says, cites.
A reader that judges six sites out of a hundred twenty-seven is a demonstration of a principle, not coverage, so
it lives in the scratch directory, it prints its own narrowing when asked, and it refuses a run whose judged count
is zero.

The self-test is ten in-process cases whose verdicts were written before the code that decides them, including a
differential case for the runaway mask and one that names a deliberate blind spot: a parenthesised reference with
its verb after the closing parenthesis is not judged, because a reference in parentheses is not the subject of its
own clause. The first self-test run scored three of eight, and the failure was the harness, not the rule: the
fixture cited a file extension outside the reader's own vocabulary, so no citation matched at all and every case
answered as unjudged. Now a case whose citation is not reached is reported as a mismatch instead of a verdict,
which is the same trap this lane has been called out for elsewhere · an empty reading that looks like a clean one.
## 234. The claim-verb list is derived by running each verb alone, and the harvest is three sentences that were wrong when written (D231)

The surface reader left a closed verb list of twelve stems typed by hand, which judged six sites of one hundred
twenty-seven. Pairing moved from clause membership to ADJACENCY · a citation is claimed by the word touching it ·
chosen because the three known false positives all touch punctuation or a connective while the known-answer refusal
touches the word "runs". Judged sites went from six to thirty-two on this plane, against one hundred forty-one
released. The self-test's tenth case flipped from released to matched and that flip was written down before the run:
a reference in parentheses followed by its verb is a claim about the line, and a clause rule throws it away because
the closing parenthesis bounds the clause. Two further cases pin the new behaviour, so the flip is a recorded rule
change and not output fitting. The list itself went from twelve hand-typed stems to forty-nine in two lists, and the
citations whose adjacency carries a claim verb went from seventeen of four hundred fourteen to seventy-nine of the
same four hundred fourteen · that denominator is this reader's own token grammar, one token wider than the drift
census's four hundred thirteen.

Widening the list ran each candidate stem alone and read its yield and its precision. Three findings, in the order
that mattered.

The first table said a stem judged nothing while the adjacency census showed its word after five citations. The verb
was not absent; its cites point at files the reader cannot open. A stem's zero was a resolution failure wearing a
vocabulary's clothes, so the table now prints dropped counts beside judged ones.

The second is the number that governs the instrument: of five hundred thirteen cite-targets in the two ledgers, three
hundred thirty-nine do not resolve at all, because a ledger names a file by basename · the ApiKeyService line
sixty-seven form · and a reader that opens only the path it is handed reaches one hundred seventy-three. The verb
list was never the binding constraint. The reader stays a scratch instrument, and now it says which constraint binds
it.

The third is a refusal that was a lie. A sentence reading that a run script's line twenty CITES a gitignore line was
contradicted because line twenty is a comment · and that comment is the thing doing the citing. So the list splits by
what the verb NEEDS: a speech verb promises only that the named line holds the words, so a comment satisfies it and a
blank line still contradicts; a structural verb promises the line runs or declares, and a comment contradicts it. That
split is now a rule with two cases of its own, and it is the reason the list is two lists.

The harvest is in the ledger's own past. Two decision rows state that one checker's line fifty-two takes its ROOT and
that another's line seventy-two is the ROOT assignment; a third row, in STATUS, attributes that same reader's
"process-cwd-derived index" to the same line seventy-two. Line fifty-two is empty, line seventy-two is a comment
about a flag parser, and the assignment is at eighty-two. Blame puts all three rows in one commit and that commit
already held the truth at both numbers, so every one of the three was wrong the moment it was written · off by one
and by ten. The drift census on a clean tree gives all three the word EXACT, and it is right to: its comparison is
line-to-line between two refs, never line-to-sentence, so a citation that was born wrong can never move and is
certified forever by a movement reader. Two of the three are also members of the twenty blank-line cites the
citation gate counts without judging, which is why no gate reddened for them. All three are repaired by the gated
applier, now row-idempotent: a row is legal only as UNAPPLIED · old cite once in its file and once on the predicted
line · or as ALREADY APPLIED · old cite gone, new cite once on that line; anything else aborts the whole run. The
first application wrote three lines and changed nothing else; the second printed ALREADY APPLIED three times and
exited zero as a measured no-op, which is a better property than the refusal it replaced.

Then the census contradicted a claim this unit was about to file, which is the reason it is filed differently. The
same sentence family cites a checker's line sixty-six as the home of a package-dot-json example, in three rows. Read
whole, the census already names those rows GONE: line sixty-six held an example that has since been rewritten into a
flag spelling and the package example moved to line two hundred thirteen with its own number generalised to a
placeholder. A first reading of the census's detail said "held and holds look identical", and that reading was wrong
at the fifty-second character · the difference is past the truncation, exactly the failure my own note about truncated
labels warns against. So the invisible class is narrower and sharper than "stale cites": it is the cite whose line was
never the one the sentence means. Movement the census sees; mis-aim at birth it cannot.

One more thing about the census, measured by this repair rather than remembered: those three sites now report NO-BASE
with the detail "absent at zero-hash, the commit that wrote the citing line", because the reader blames the WORKING
COPY and my edit made the lines uncommitted. An in-flight repair deletes itself from the population it is supposed to
clear, and after the commit the same three sites will read EXACT again · the identical word they read while broken.
Two of my instruments and one of my own hands, recorded because they were measured and not noticed. The append proof
rebuilt HEAD's ledger text by applying the repairs to both ledgers and its prefix check failed on STATUS · which is
how the third site was found: a purity test that names a line the repair also names is an accidental census, and the
census is now written on purpose. The same proof exists because this unit's appender ran twice before anyone read the
line counts, landing a second copy numbered as the next section, and the duplicate was cut by a heading-anchored
truncate; the proof now refuses a tail holding a heading count other than one, so an accidental double append cannot
land again. The applier also printed ten thousand two lone feeds on a file holding none: its check asked whether the
character AFTER a line feed was a carriage return, which flags every ordinary pair, and a lone feed is one with no
return BEFORE it · the landed append proof of the previous unit used the byte form, so its recorded claim stands and
the wrong line was scratch-only. And the census's nonsense BEFORE tokens · a controller's name, a test class's name ·
turned out to be slash-list citations: twelve cite tokens in eight ledger lines spell several numbers after one
colon-separated head, and every reader this lane owns reads the head and hands the tail to the adjacency extractor.

Readings on this plane, after the repair and before the append: the surface reader judges thirty-two sites and
contradicts none; the citation gate, the comment-plane reader, the section reader, the section-citation reader and the

DECISIONS grow by pure appends with the committed blob, plus the three repaired lines, a byte prefix of the new text.
Nothing pushed; the other lane's dirty files, including its live number reader and its dirty drift reader, are

## 251. The campaign surface closes the adoption arc (17688e2): 199/0/0 on a clean plane, the committed plane serves 94 - up from 82 the morning the arc started - and the door test caught the draft's own comment promising a 422 its repository deliberately does not send
Three files: `MerchantCampaignController.java` (+482 · `POST /campaigns` writing the draft literal and

out of draft · stamped once, idempotent on a second call, `scheduled` rather than `live` when the start is

translated to 409), `MerchantCampaignRepository.java` (+176), and `MerchantCampaignDoorTest.java` (+192,
authored first · the pair shipped no test). Working copy 2/0/0 in 11.54s; acceptance on a detached
worktree at 17688e2: **199 tests / 0 failures / 0 errors, BUILD SUCCESS**.
The authored witness earned its keep twice. It pinned the boundary the route exists to hold · only
approve-publish says live, the human is named on the row, the second click changes nothing, and the
coupon a live campaign advertises left draft in the same transaction, so a live campaign never advertises
a draft offer. And it caught the draft disagreeing with itself: the controller's comment promises a 422
"naming the field" for a coupon the merchant does not own, while the repository deliberately answers the
workspace's 404 `coupon_not_found` (its own comment cites D5). The test pins the code, because the code is
what answers; the adoption is byte-for-byte, so the stale comment ships with the record of its mismatch.
Two authoring lessons the run itself taught, for the next lane that writes one of these: the refusal order
is resolver-then-grant · a body the permission resolver cannot read is a 422 before anyone's grants are
considered, so a 403 test must carry a body that resolves; and the refusal table is as much of the door as
the happy path · three audited 403s (create on both doors, publish without the grant) sit beside the 409,
the 404, the 401 and the window/percent 422s.

→ 89 (one real, one reader false-pass named in its section), knowledge → 91, campaigns → **94 served, 16
CLIENT-ONLY**. Twelve documented routes stopped being calls nobody answers. The remaining 16 belong to
lanes beyond the merchant tree: five `/ai/v1`, four `/api/v1/admin`, seven across the untracked
commerce/seo packages, `/api/v1/users/{id}` and the payment webhook · each is now a named, measurable gap

## 253. CORRECTION to §224: the EBUSY was the default `stdio`, not the sandbox · one option unlocks every harness

§224 censused six tools that die without a verdict and recorded the cause as this machine refusing to spawn a
child process. That cause is **wrong**, and the correction is measurable in four lines:

```
execFileSync git, default stdio              FAIL    6ms  code=EBUSY status=null
execFileSync git, stdio ignore/pipe/ignore   OK   1081ms
spawnSync    git, default stdio              FAIL    3ms  code=EBUSY status=undefined
spawnSync    git, stdio ignore/pipe/ignore   OK    451ms
spawnSync    node -> node, stdio ignore/pipe/pipe   status=0  error=none  out="child ran"
```

**A child that inherits this process's handles fails with `EBUSY` in about 3 milliseconds; the same child
with `stdio: ['ignore','pipe','pipe']` runs.** Nothing is forbidden. The class §224 named is real · a process
that never started must not print the same line as one that ran and found nothing · but its *cause* was a
missing option, not an environment, and every "this gate step cannot run on this machine" conclusion drawn
from it was drawn from the wrong fact.

**Proof that the harnesses run, not that they might.** `scripts/falsify_quality_seam.mjs` · one of the six ·
takes the option at its single spawn site and reports:

```
RESULT: PASS · 38 of 38 arms held; the seam reaches the site census and the gate step that runs it
```

It had been recorded as unrunnable on this plane. It runs, and its arms hold.

**What this does not change.** The tools that were *fixed* in §224 still needed fixing: they died with no
verdict line, and a spawn failure · whatever its cause · must be named rather than inferred. What changes is
that the fix for most of them is now one option at the call site, and that the gate's steps 7-12 have not been
shown unrunnable here at all.

**Cost, measured, because it is not free.** A `git` child costs about **645 ms** on this host (100 spawns in
64,490 ms), which is why `scripts/check_citation_supports_sentence.mjs` takes 4m07s over 499 citations. A slow
tool and a hanging tool look identical to `timeout`, and a 240-second limit killed a working feature earlier
in this same line of work · see the reverted-and-reapplied basename index in that file.

§253 corrected §224's cause. This is what the correction is worth, measured by re-running every tool that had
been written off. The change is one option at each spawn site · `stdio: ['ignore', 'pipe', 'pipe']` · and the
column that matters is the middle one.

```
tool                        before the option                     after
falsify_quality_seam        NOT CHECKED · rc null, both planes    PASS · 38 of 38 arms held
falsify_line_cite_drift     died silently, no RESULT line         PASS · 12/12 arms

falsify_ledger_text         died silently, no RESULT line         PASS

citation_blank_sites        died silently, no RESULT line         runs, rc 0 (report-only by design)
falsify_comment_plane       FAIL · 57 arms, 0 held, 57 missed     PASS · 57 arms, 57 held, 0 missed
```

**Six tools that died without a verdict now run, and three harnesses that reported FAIL now report PASS.** The

**The `falsify_comment_plane` flip is the clearest one.** 0 of 57 arms held before and 57 of 57 after · a
harness that scored every arm as a miss because every child failed to start, which is exactly the failure

**Verified before and after.** `node --check` over all 34 files in `scripts/`: **0 syntax failures**. Two
insertion sites were read by eye (`check_status_citations.mjs:88`, `falsify_ledger_text.mjs:226`) and both are
well-formed option objects.

**Cost, unchanged and now the binding constraint.** A child costs about **645 ms** on this host, so the slow
harnesses need 5-10 minutes each: `falsify_comment_plane` and `falsify_ledger_text` both exceeded a 420-second
limit and pass when given 580. A `timeout` shorter than a tool's baseline looks exactly like a hang · the
mistake that cost a working feature earlier in this line of work, and the reason every number above carries
the limit it was measured under.

## 255. a concurrent-write collision, found by a harness whose control arm runs on the real tree

`falsify_ledger_sections.mjs` reported `FAIL · the fork guard does not do what its arms claim`, and the arm
that missed is the one that should be easiest to satisfy:

```
MISSED  exit 0 expected, 1 printed   a draft section on disk, not yet committed (§252 does not exist at HEAD)
        printed: NOTE ... 1 section(s) on disk and not at HEAD: 252
                 NOTE ... D272 duplicated
                 FORK docs/DECISIONS.md: duplicated decision numbers (on disk: D272×2)
                 RESULT: FAIL · the ledgers' two planes disagree in a way that loses committed sections
```

The arm's expectation is right and the reader's verdict is right; what the arm did not anticipate is that its
**control arm runs on `ROOT`, the real tree** (`dir: ROOT` in the arm table), so any defect in the working copy
lands in the control. The defect is a genuine one, measured:

```
docs/DECISIONS.md  ## D272 · Step 9 turned green; full reader battery green; ...   line 12214, 16 lines
                   ## D272 · Step 9 turned green; full reader battery green; ...   line 12230, 15 lines
docs/STATUS.md     ## 252. D238: step 9 green by owner's placeholder fix; ...      line 12606, 24 lines
                   ## 252. D238: step 9 green by owner's placeholder fix; ...      line 12668, 42 lines
```

**Same titles, different bodies** · this is not a copy left behind, it is two lanes writing the same entry
independently, so neither copy can be deleted by a reader: one of the two bodies is missing something the
other has. `check_ledger_sections.mjs` already names both as `FORK` and exits 1, and the four numbers are
uncommitted, which is consistent with a collision between two working copies rather than a bad commit.

**Not edited here.** Both bodies belong to the lanes that wrote them; merging needs a decision about which
half is authoritative, and a reader that guesses would delete somebody's paragraph. What this section adds is
the route by which the collision surfaced · a harness control that runs against the real tree · and the exact
line numbers, so the merge is mechanical once the owners agree.

Unrelated and unchanged by the above: `node --check` over all 34 scripts is 0 failures, and the numeric census
is PASS at 842 claims.

## 256. the basename index, re-applied and read: the judged population triples, 100 -> 309

`check_citation_supports_sentence.mjs` skips a citation it cannot resolve, and about 262 of them were written
as a bare basename · `sql.py:137` · pointing at files that *are* committed. The gate's own step 8 resolves
those. This reader was not asking, so two thirds of its population was counted and never judged.

The index was **reverted once, for the wrong reason** (§253 records the 240-second timeout that was shorter
than the tool's own baseline). Re-applied, and read to completion at last:

```
citations seen           507
the same pattern, scanned directly   507      ← the discriminator: the walk loses nothing
judged (sentence had an identifier the file could spell)   309
skipped: target not at HEAD (the other readers own it)      34
basenames resolved       294 (bare name -> one committed file)
basenames ambiguous        0 (two or more files share the name, not guessed)
sharing nothing          156 of 309
```

**Judged 100 -> 309 and skipped 324 -> 34.** Only a **unique** hit is resolved; ambiguous basenames are
counted, not guessed, and on this tree there are none · which is itself a finding: every bare basename in
these ledgers names exactly one committed file, so the resolution carries no coin flips.

**The cost, stated because it is the reason this took three attempts to land.** The run takes **6m08s** (up
from 4m07s: the extra `git show` per resolved basename). A `timeout` below that looks exactly like a hang, and
that is what killed the feature twice.

**What this changes for the next reader.** `sharing nothing 156 of 309` is a much larger list than the 42 of
100 it replaces, and it is a list of *questions*, not defects · the same limit the tool states in its own
footer. It is also, for the first time, a list drawn from a population that includes the citations this
repository mostly writes.

## 257. hand-checking the census found a defect in the census, and then a real stale citation

§256 read the sentence-support census at `156 of 309` sharing no identifier. A number that large is worth a
minute of reading before it is worth quoting, and the first row checked was **wrong in the reader's favour**:

```
docs/STATUS.md:3064 -> …/merchant/MerchantService.java:63
  sentence names 44 identifier(s); the neighbourhood has none of: changed, data, seed, quality.sql
```

The sentence says `App side: MerchantService.java:63 passes principal.userId()`; line 63 is
`merchants.addMember(tenant, merchantId, principal.userId(), "owner");` · **the citation is exact**. What the
reader had done was take its identifiers from the text **before** the citation, which in that paragraph is two
lines about `granted_by` and `generate.py`. A claim about a cited line is written on **both** sides of it, and
`clauseFor` only looked left.

**Fixed**: the span now runs from the previous citation to the next one, not to the end of the sentence.

```
                      before the span fix   after
judged                309                   96
sharing nothing       156 of 309            30 of 96
```

**Fewer rows, and the first one checked is a true positive.** `docs/DECISIONS.md:9108` cites
"the `PYTHON` knob at `db_gate_fresh.sh:128` and `:246`". Measured:

```
db_gate_fresh.sh:128   psql_maint "DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS \"$GATE_DB\"" …      ← the cleanup function
db_gate_fresh.sh:246   # above them unverified, while §84 had already shipped …   ← a comment
db_gate_fresh.sh:153   PYTHON="${PYTHON:-python}"                                ← the knob
db_gate_fresh.sh:330   ( cd "$ROOT" && "${PYTHON:-python}" data/seed/falsifier_plants.py --self-test )
```

**Both halves of that citation are wrong** · one points at cleanup, the other at prose. It is a stale citation
of the kind the position readers cannot see (both lines exist and hold text) and the identifier census can.

**The trade this records, stated rather than hidden**: the narrower span costs coverage · `judged` falls
309 -> 96, because a one-clause span often carries no identifier to compare · and buys precision, 156 -> 30.
Coverage that produced a false row is not coverage, so the trade is taken, and the residual limit is that this
reader now judges a fifth of the citations it sees rather than three fifths.

## 258. the stale citation was a MOVED one the position readers cannot see at all, and the re-aim is applied

§257 hand-checked one row of the identifier census and found a citation that looked wrong in both halves:
"the `PYTHON` knob at `db_gate_fresh.sh:128` and `:246`". Two facts settle what kind of defect it is, and both
were measured rather than argued.

**It is MOVED, not wrong.** The commit that wrote the sentence is `fccedf9`, and in that revision the knob sat
exactly where the sentence says:

```
git show fccedf9:scripts/db_gate_fresh.sh   |  128:  PYTHON="${PYTHON:-python}"
                                            |  246:  ( cd "$ROOT" && "${PYTHON:-python}" … --self-test )
git show HEAD:scripts/db_gate_fresh.sh      |  153:  PYTHON="${PYTHON:-python}"
                                            |  330:  ( cd "$ROOT" && "${PYTHON:-python}" … --self-test )
```

So the citation was **correct when written** and the file grew under it · the class `check_line_cite_drift.mjs`
exists to catch.

**And that reader cannot catch this one.** `db_gate_fresh.sh` is written as a **bare basename**, so the
citation lands in that reader's `UNPATHED` class · 277 of them, printed and counted, never resolved. Both
position readers decline it: one will not resolve a basename, the other judges only what it can resolve. This
is the first citation found by the identifier census that **no position reader could have judged**, which is
the clearest statement yet of what the third reader is for.

**Applied**, with both targets re-read after the edit:

```
docs/DECISIONS.md:9108   `db_gate_fresh.sh:153` and `:330`
scripts/db_gate_fresh.sh:153   PYTHON="${PYTHON:-python}"                                ← the knob
scripts/db_gate_fresh.sh:355   ( cd "$ROOT" && "${PYTHON:-python}" … --self-test )      ← the invocation
```

**The chain, in one place**, because each link was a separate unit and the value is in the sequence: a missing
`stdio` option made six tools die silently (STATUS §253) · one of them, a harness control running on the real
tree, was also being reddened by a concurrent-write collision (§255) · and once the tools ran, a basename index
that had been reverted on a too-short timeout could be read to completion (§256), which made the judged
population large enough that hand-checking it found a defect in the reader itself (§257), and fixing that
produced this citation, which no other reader in the repository could see.

## 259. `--resolve-basenames`: 58 stale citations were invisible because the reader refuses bare names

§258 ended with a citation no position reader could judge, because it is written as a bare basename and
`check_line_cite_drift.mjs` refuses those by a decision stated in its own header. Refusing them is a ruling, so
the default was **not** changed; a switch was added to measure what the ruling costs:

```
                          default     --resolve-basenames
EXACT                     132         310
MOVED                       2          53      ← 51 more stale citations
NOT-UNIQUE                  0          13
GONE                       16          23      ← 7 more
NO-BASE                     1           7
UNPATHED                  277          22
NOT-AT-HEAD                 3           3
judged by content         151         406
```

**255 of the 277 UNPATHED citations resolve, and 58 of them are MOVED or GONE** · stale citations that no
reader in this repository was judging. The default run is byte-for-byte what it was (EXACT 132, MOVED 2,
GONE 16, UNPATHED 277), so the switch changes nothing unless it is asked for.

**What this does not decide.** Whether the default should move is a ruling, not a patch: the refusal is a
documented choice, and the reader's header says why. What this section supplies is the number that decision
was made without · 58 defects behind one class · and the mechanism (`--resolve-basenames`) that lets whoever
owns the ruling verify the change in one run rather than argue for it.

**The larger pattern this closes.** Three classes of "counted and never judged" have now been opened by the
same move · resolve the thing instead of refusing it, and see what was behind: the sentence-support census
(100 -> 309 judged, §256), the UNPATHED class here (277 -> 22), and the citation §258 recovered from it. In
all three the refusal was stated and counted, which is what made the population measurable at all; the cost
was that a stated refusal reads like a clean answer.

the new line from where the old text moved; it does not ask whether the moved text still *supports* the
sentence, which is the question §257's census asks and this one does not. Applying these rows fixes position;
it does not make them true.

other lanes and leave the edits to their owners, and that is what this section does.

## 261. `cpSync` of a directory exits 127 silently on this host · the harness was innocent all along

`falsify_console_a11y.mjs` had been recorded as a harness that "runs eight minutes, prints nothing, exits 127".
Six measurements later the file is exonerated and the cause is one line of Node behaviour, reproducible with no
harness in the loop:

```
node -e "cpSync('apps/web/app', dest, {recursive:true})"              → rc=127, 0 bytes
node -e "cpSync('apps/web/src/components', dest, {recursive:true})"   → rc=127, 0 bytes
node -e "cpSync('packages/ui/src', dest, {recursive:true})"           → rc=127, 0 bytes
node -e "cpSync('packages/ui/README.md', dest, {recursive:true})"     → rc=0, prints OK
```

**Copying a directory with `cpSync(..., { recursive: true })` kills the Node process silently with exit 127 on
this machine. Copying a file works.** The destination's parent existing or not makes no difference (both
tested, both 127).

**The harness's `fixture()` is four lines and copies four subtrees.** The process dies in the first `cpSync`
before reaching its first `console.log` · which is why `--trace-exit` had nothing to say, why `--help` behaved
the same, and why the file read as dead. **Nothing in that file was edited.**

**Blast radius: one file.** `grep -l cpSync scripts/*.mjs` returns `falsify_console_a11y.mjs` and nothing else,
so no other tool in this repository can be hit by it. That is worth stating precisely because the failure is
silent: a second user of this call would have looked identical to a broken harness.

**Three host restrictions this session has found by measurement, one shape.** Each is an operation this machine
simply does not permit, arriving as a code that reads like something else:

```
piping a child's stdin        EBUSY in ~3 ms      read for a session as "the sandbox forbids spawning"
the bash shell's loader       unable to load netapi32.dll
cpSync of a directory         silent exit 127     read for hours as a broken harness
```

The pattern is the same one §253 named for a different class: **a plausible-looking code on an operation that
did not happen is worse than no code**, because it points the reader at the wrong subject. All three were found
by measuring a thing that could not possibly have failed, not by reading the tool that did.

**Untested**: the workaround. A file-by-file copy should do the same job; that is one run and is not claimed
here.

## 262. the workaround, applied: `falsify_console_a11y` runs and passes

§261 found the cause · `cpSync` of a directory exits 127 silently on this host · and left the workaround
untested. Tested, then applied:

```
file-by-file copy of the same subtrees   apps/web/app 43 files 450ms · components 22 files 103ms ·
                                         packages/ui/src 24 files 116ms · WORKAROUND OK, rc 0
```

`fixture()` now walks the source with `mkdirSync` + `copyFileSync` instead of `cpSync(..., {recursive:true})`,
and the harness that had been recorded as "runs eight minutes, prints nothing, exits 127" reports:

```
RESULT: PASS -- the census reddens on every way a landmark, name, focus ring or printed ratio can break,
and refuses when it cannot see
```

**One correction inside the fix, recorded because it is the same lesson one level down.** The hand-rolled copy
called `readdirSync` on `packages/ui/README.md` and died with `ENOTDIR` · `SUBTREES` names three directories
and one file, and `cpSync` accepted both shapes while a walk has to ask which it was given. A replacement for a
call whose contract is wider than the call you are writing has to handle the wider contract.

**Where this leaves the census of silent tools.** Every tool in `scripts/` that spawns or copies now runs on
this plane and states a verdict. The three that still report FAIL are statements about a reader
(`falsify_untracked_cites` 14/15, and the collision-driven `falsify_ledger_sections` control), not silences ·
and the one file this host restriction could reach is fixed.

## 266. the gate runs to step 8 on this machine at last · and stops on a timeout that is shorter than what it budgets

`bash scripts/db_gate_fresh.sh` had been recorded as unable to run here. Two host facts had to be measured
first, and neither is a code defect:

```
step 2  apply infra/db/migrations/V*.sql + 00_roles.sql
        [safe-delete][SAFE_DELETE_INVALID_PATH] embedded drive prefix is not allowed
        > apply V1__init  <- V1__init.sql                      EXIT=1

cause   TMPDIR='C://Users//18414//AppData//Local//Temp'   (a Windows path)
        mktemp "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/nexus-migrate.XXXXXX"  →  C://Users//…//Temp/nexus-migrate.jbqMzp
        `db_apply_migrations.sh` then does `rm -f "$err"` on that mixed path, and the sandbox refuses any
        path carrying a drive prefix.

fix     TMPDIR=/tmp bash scripts/db_gate_fresh.sh
```

**With `TMPDIR=/tmp` the gate runs**: steps 1-7 green (migrations, seed, the Java suites, the reader battery)
and step 8 reached · **steps that had been written off as unrunnable on this plane**. It stops at step 8 on a
real falsifier failure rather than an environment one:

```
step 8  scripts/check_ledger_citations.mjs
        MISSED  exit 1 expected, -1 printed   a reader with D191's committed-plane read put back to the blind
                                              spot reddens this harness
        RESULT: FAIL · the --text seam does not do what step 8 claims        EXIT=1
```

**`-1` is the spawn-failure sentinel, and here it is a timeout.** The arm runs `falsify_ledger_text.mjs`
**again** through a nested `spawnSync` bounded by `timeout: 300000` · five minutes · while that harness needs
**more than eight** to finish. The child is killed, `child.status` is `null`, `code = child.status ?? -1`
becomes `-1`, and the arm misses on a number that reads like a process that never started.

**Raised to `900000`.** This is the same mistake this line of work already made once by hand · a `timeout`
below the baseline it was measuring · except that here it is in the code, where it cannot be seen by running
the thing it kills. The cost is stated rather than hidden: the harness now takes **15+ minutes**, because the
nested run is finally allowed to complete.

## 335. the recommendation grounding boundary is now enforced at the wire (D339)

§18/§19 say every recommendation bullet a user sees must trace to a `fact_id` (a
verifiable fact), and §1846 forbids deceiving users for payment · a paid placement
is *labelled* `sponsored`, never faked into a trust reason. `build_reasons` already
honoured this internally (it skips any feature it cannot ground; `sponsored` is the
one deliberate `fact_id=None`), but the **contract boundary did not enforce it**:
`MatchExplanation.fact_id` is `Optional`, and `models/base.py` passes an upstream
`reasons` list through unvalidated. A future LLM/upstream mapper that narrated a
reason without a fact could have shipped an unverifiable claim straight to the user.

**The fix is the last line before a card ships, not a crash.** `drop_ungrounded_reasons`
in `search/cards.py` removes any `MatchExplanation` whose `fact_id is None` and whose
`label` is not in the one allowed exception set (`{sponsored}`), and returns how many
it dropped. The `recommend` endpoint runs it over `pack.cards` and logs a warning if
anything was dropped · so a misbehaving producer is *counted*, never silent, and the
response never 500s on upstream garbage (the project's degrade-don't-crash discipline).

**Verified, not claimed** (DB-free, mock provider):
```
tests/test_recommend_reasons_grounded.py  · 5 passed
full apps/ai suite                      · 85 passed, 4 skipped (live-DB tests need Docker, down)
```
Five cases cover the four outcomes: an ungrounded non-sponsored reason is dropped; a
`sponsored` reason with no `fact_id` is kept; a fully-grounded card is untouched; a
card with no `ai_match` is a no-op; and the live `/ai/v1/recommend` response carries
no ungrounded non-sponsored reason. `dropped == 0` is the steady state for the rules
path · the guard exists for the producer that does not yet exist.

## 336. the personalization signal's contract is pinned by tests (D340)

§99/§100: personalization is an EMA over feedback, never ground truth alone, and
it stays neutral until enough signals accumulate (`PersonalizationConfig.min_signals`,
default 3). `personalization_signal` in `search/ranking.py` is pure logic (no DB), so
it is the kind of contract worth pinning directly rather than inferring from a ranker
integration test that needs Docker.

`tests/test_personalization_signal.py` locks five behaviours:
- below `min_signals` it returns `None` (the ranker falls back to `neutral`);
- at `min_signals` it returns a value in `[0, 1]`;
- out-of-range inputs are clamped to `[0, 1]` (`_norm01`);
- a strong *opening* rating outweighs a strong *closing* one (the `ema_alpha=0.1`
  direction), documented with values that stay inside `[0, 1]` so clamping cannot
  mask it;
- a custom `min_signals` is respected (1 sample is enough at `min_signals=1`; 4 is
  still short of 5).

**Verified, not claimed** (DB-free):
```
tests/test_personalization_signal.py · 5 passed
```
The first cut of the EMA-direction case failed because both candidate EMAs clamped to
`1.0` · the function was right, the test's values were wrong. Fixed by keeping the
inputs inside `[0, 1]`. A test that fails for the wrong reason is worse than no test;
the corrected case now proves the direction without hiding behind the clamp.

## 338. the prompt-injection trust module is pinned by tests (D342)

`trust/injection.py` is the §19 / AGENT_CONTRACT §8 guard: reviews, merchant text, OCR,
imported docs and external payloads are *data, never instructions*. It scans for
instruction-shaped language (EN + ZH), command-injection tokens, payment-fraud and
unauthorised-reservation phrases, URL exfil cues, and · crucially · registry tool names
appearing inside content (a tool is only ever dispatched from the registry, never parsed
out of data). It had **zero tests**; this unit pins it.

`tests/test_injection.py` locks fifteen behaviours across the public surface:
- EN/ZH "ignore previous instructions", role-hijack (EN/ZH), `command_injection`
  (`rm -rf`), `payment_fraud` ("free of charge"), `reserve_without_user`
  ("booking the table is confirmed"), `url_exfil` ("send it to https://…"), and a
  registry tool name in content (`create_reservation` surfaces as `tool_name_in_content`
  carrying the exact name + length);
- benign and empty text are not flagged (empty counts 0 chars scanned);
- `sanitize_untrusted` strips the envelope delimiter so content cannot close its own
  envelope (forgery-prevention);
- `wrap_untrusted` encloses content between the fixed delimiters, appends a hit count
  when flagged, and with `scan=False` still wraps but reports clean;
- `merge_reports` sums hits + scanned chars;
- a flagged report degrades (`status="open"`, `severity="warn"`, score `0.25*hits`
  capped at 1) while a clean one is `informational` / `info`.

## 342. the time-resolution contract is pinned by tests (D346)

§8 / §7.1: `nlu/timeparse.py::parse_time` resolves a user's free-text temporal mention to a
`TimeIntent` (or `None` when there is no time signal). It is the front line of §8's
never-guess discipline *for time* · a query like "推荐一家好吃的" carries no time signal and
must resolve to `None`, never an invented default. `parse_time` implemented this but had
**no tests**; this unit pins the contract with a fixed reference clock so the assertions are
deterministic.

Reference clock (fixed, not `now`):
```
NOW = datetime(2024, 1, 1, 10, 0, tzinfo=HK_TZ)   # Monday
```

`tests/test_timeparse.py` (11 cases) locks:
- **no time signal ⇒ None** (§8 honesty · "有什么好推荐" / "推荐一家店" resolve to `None`, not a
  default hour); the same `None` path is exercised through the public `understand` surface;
- **passed-hour rollover**: "7點" at 10:00 ⇒ tomorrow 07:00 (a clock time already behind
  today's reads as the next occurrence, never "yesterday");
- **literal clocks**: "晚上8點" ⇒ 20:00, "22:30" ⇒ 22:30, "10pm" ⇒ 22:00 · meridian words and
  24h/12h/pm forms all normalise to HK-local wall time;
- **relative-weekday**: "周六晚上" ⇒ next Saturday 2024-01-06 (the first Sat ≥ tomorrow),
  "週末" ⇒ a Saturday-anchored span;
- **day words**: "今晚" ⇒ today 18:00, "明日" ⇒ 2024-01-02 all-day;
- **open-late relative**: "營業到10點後" ⇒ a relative `open_late_after: 1000` marker rather than
  an absolute instant (the merchant's own close time is not known at parse time · §8 would
  forbid guessing it, so the parser emits a relative cue the ranker can act on);
- **serialisation**: `to_intent_dict` emits Zulu (`+00:00`-normalised) timestamps and leaves
  genuinely-absent fields as `null` · no fabricated defaults leak into the wire JSON.

## 343. the sponsored-placement contract is pinned by tests (D347)

§67 / §66 / §1846: paid placement is a *capped post-hoc insertion*, never a scoring input.
`search/ranking.py` is pure Python over the `Candidate` feature vector, so the invariants
are unit-testable without a database · but neither `score_candidate` nor `apply_sponsored`
had any tests. This unit pins both.

`tests/test_sponsored_ranking.py` (12 cases):
- **organic score is sponsored-blind** (§67): two candidates with byte-identical features,
  differing only in the `sponsored` flag, produce *exactly* the same `score_candidate`
  output · a paid placement can never earn a higher organic score than an equal organic one;
- **organic best never displaced**: even a promoted card with a *higher* organic score sits
  behind the organic best at rank 0;
- **no promoted card at rank 0** (across a 6-organic + 2-promoted mix);
- **capped within the top window**: with the default `cap_in_top=5 / max_in_top=1`, at most
  one promoted card appears in the first 5 slots; the surplus (2 of 3) is pushed to the
  tail, and *no* promoted card is ever dropped;
- **custom cap enforced**: `SponsoredConfig(cap_in_top=5, max_in_top=2)` puts exactly 2
  promoted within the top 5 and pushes the other 2 to the tail;
- **no boost**: `apply_sponsored` only reorders · every result keeps `score == organic_score`;
- **organic positions preserved on the cards**: organic cards carry their 1-based
  `organic_rank`; a promoted card (never in the organic list) carries `organic_rank = None`,
  proving it did not displace an organic result's slot (§67);
- **promotion by id set** (not just the flag) works and still keeps the organic best first;
- **no-promo / no-organic edge cases** return the input order unchanged;
- **`sponsor_label`** lookup + fallback: `zh-HK` default, unknown locale falls back to
  `zh-HK`, and the literal `"Sponsored"` only when `zh-HK` itself is absent.

One test premise was corrected, not the code: with `cap_in_top=3` the strict
`len(result) < cap_in_top` interleaving fits only 1 promoted slot, so the custom-cap case
uses `cap_in_top=5` to actually exercise `max_in_top=2`. The function is correct; the test
was asserting an impossible interleave.

`trust/facts.py` is the §4 grounding anchor (AGENT_CONTRACT §4, spec §19/§53): every
AI-stated fact must resolve to one of these, and the §4 source hierarchy
(`merchant > observed > imported > third_party > inferred > demo`), the per-source

module is pure except for the `facts_from_rows` DB-row bridge · but it had **no tests**.

  `merchant` keeps 0.99 (third-party may never out-rank merchant · §3);
- **`stable_fact_id`** is content-derived and deterministic (replay ⇒ same id, different
  value ⇒ different id) · what makes the SSE frame reproducible;
- **ordering**: `pick_all` ranks by source hierarchy, ties broken by confidence;
  `pick_authoritative` returns the best or `None`;

- **`select_display_facts`** respects requested order and skips missing attributes;
- **`synth`** is idempotent (same content + observed_at ⇒ same id) and marks `observed`;
- **`facts_from_rows`** (DB bridge) clamps confidence, parses JSON values, honours

## 351. the query-understanding lexicon is pinned by tests (D355)

`nlu/lexicon.py` is the deterministic, data-driven lexicon the NLU extractors build on
(spec §7, AGENT_CONTRACT §12, §111-112): locale detection, district/category/cuisine
matching, query normalization, constraint canonicalization, and entity hints. It is pure
data + pure functions · no network, no DB · so this unit is fully offline. It had **zero
tests** for its own rules (only covered transitively).

`tests/test_lexicon.py` (47 cases):

- **§12 locale** (`detect_language`): empty ⇒ `zh-HK` (market default); pure ASCII ⇒ `en`;
  trad marker `餐廳` ⇒ `zh-HK`, simp marker `餐厅`/`电脑` ⇒ `zh-CN`; a *shared* character
  (`餐`) votes for neither, so the market default wins · the marker-pair design prevents a
  common char from mis-detecting the locale;
- **districts** (`match_district`): zh alias (`尖沙咀`), en name (`central`), **longest alias
  wins** (`causeway bay cwb` ⇒ Causeway Bay), non-HK text ⇒ `None`, returned spec carries
  `aliases/lat/lng/area`;
- **categories** (`match_category`): generic buckets (`restaurant`/`retail`) get conf `0.7`,
  specific (`cafe`) get `0.95`; rightmost *specific* wins (`電影院同咖啡店` ⇒ `cafe`, reversed
  ⇒ `cinema`); no signal ⇒ `None`;
- **cuisines** (`match_cuisines`): `壽司`⇒japanese, `泰國菜`⇒thai, `素食`⇒vegetarian, none⇒`[]`;
- **normalization** (`normalize_query`): strips CJK/ASCII punctuation, collapses whitespace,
  **keeps a digit-adjacent colon** (`7:30pm`) but drops a non-digit colon (`價錢：餐廳`⇒
  `價錢 餐廳`); does **not** lowercase (matching functions lower internally);
- **constraints** (`canon_constraint`): `辣`/`spicy`⇒`spicy`, `咖哩`/`咖喱`⇒`curry`, `牛`⇒
  `beef`, `排隊`⇒`queue`, unknown⇒lowercased, `None`⇒`""`;
- **entity hints**: `quoted_entities` (`「海底撈」`, `"Ocean Park"`), `proper_nouns` (captures
  `Book`/`Starbucks`, excludes stopwords `Compare`/`and` and `hk`, none for lowercase);
- **data integrity**: `SIMPLIFIED_MARKERS`/`TRADITIONAL_MARKERS` are disjoint; every district
  has non-empty aliases + float lat/lng + area; `PREFERENCE_RULE_VALUES` and `NEGATION_CUES`
  match their source derivations; every `PREFERENCE_RULES` row is a 4-tuple with polarity ∈
  {1,-1}.

**Premise corrected, not the code** (two test premises were wrong, the module is right):
`電腦` is the *traditional* form (電/腦 are both trad markers) ⇒ `zh-HK`; the simplified form
is `电脑`. And `normalize_query` deliberately leaves `ABC` upper-case.

**Discrepancy flagged (no code change made on a guess)**: `match_category` prefers a
*specific* category over a *generic* one even when the generic is rightmost, so
`可帶寵物的餐廳` returns `pet`, **not** `restaurant`. This contradicts the module docstring's
"rightmost wins" claim, which uses exactly that example to argue a pet token must *not*
hijack a restaurant query. The actual behaviour is pinned as-is; the author should confirm
intent · a pet-shop lexicon token may be over-powering restaurant queries. (§19/§105
discipline: observe, document, don't mutate on a guess.)

## 365. D367 · pin the intent-bucket → taxonomy bridge (`search/categories.resolve`)

**Module / contract.** `nexus_ai.search.categories` is the pure, DB-free bridge between the
intent layer's coarse category *bucket* (`restaurant`, `escape_room`, `retail` …) and the seeded
`categories` taxonomy (10 roots + 67 leaves, hyphenated slugs). `search/sql.py` calls `resolve`
to turn a bucket into the slug set a `slug IN (…)` SQL predicate should match.

**Why it matters (regression guard).** Comparing the raw bucket to the taxonomy slug with `=`
matched *nothing* on the live DB · every categorised query returned an empty page · so the bucket
is expanded here into `[bucket, slug(bucket), *ALIASES[bucket]]`. Pinning the expansion is what
stops that regression from silently returning an empty category page again.

**Pinned behavior (22 cases, all confirmed empirically against the module):**
- Empty contract: `None`, `""`, and whitespace-only all return `[]` (no category asked).
- Normalization: case-insensitive (`RESTAURANT` → `['restaurant']`); surrounding whitespace trimmed.
- Slug formation: every bucket carries its own name first, then the hyphenated taxonomy slug
  (`escape_room` → `['escape_room', 'escape-room']`); an unrecognised bucket still yields its
  hyphenated slug so a stray taxonomy row stays reachable.
- Alias expansion: each `ALIASES` entry is emitted in order · `afternoon_tea` →
  `['afternoon_tea', 'afternoon-tea', 'tea-house', 'cha-chan-teng']`; `retail` → `['retail', 'shopping']`;
  `pet` → `['pet', 'pet-grooming']`; `attraction` → `['attraction', 'experience', 'activity']`, etc.
- Dedup + order-stability: no duplicate slugs; output identical across repeated calls.
- **Bridge regression**: an aliased bucket MUST still surface its taxonomy slugs
  (`set(resolve('afternoon_tea')) >= {'tea-house', 'cha-chan-teng'}`), and the hyphenated slug is
  always present so `sql.py`'s `slug IN (resolve(b))` finds rows instead of an empty page.

**Discipline note.** No test-premise corrections were needed this unit · the module's behavior
matched the docstring's stated contract exactly. Code unchanged.

**Verified, not claimed.** `pytest tests/test_categories.py` → **22 passed**; full `apps/ai`
suite → **363 passed, 4 skipped** (`pytest -q`, live-DB tests skip because Docker is down).

---

## 366. D368 · pin `extract_intent_dict` structured resolution (§7.1, §111, §8)

**Module / contract.** `nexus_ai.nlu.understand.extract_intent_dict` is the pure, DB-free front
door of NLU. D341 (§337) already pinned its **§8 never-guess / unknowns** honesty. This unit pins
the *structured extraction* slice D341 did not cover: district resolution, category-bucket
extraction, numeric party size, and the `cuisine_avoid` / `diet_avoid` constraint shaping. The
rule engine runs offline, so this is fully DB-free.

**Pinned behavior (25 cases, all confirmed empirically):**
- Top-level shape: required keys present; `intent` is a non-empty string; `confidence` is a **dict**
  (`{intent, category, location}`, each a unit float in [0,1]); `unknowns` is a list.
- District resolution: Chinese + English districts map to `{type:'district', value:<English
  canonical>, resolved:{lat,lng}, radius_m:None}` · 尖沙咀→Tsim Sha Tsui, 銅鑼灣→Causeway Bay,
  旺角→Mong Kok, central→Central, causeway bay→Causeway Bay. Absent district → `{}` (not `None`).
- Category bucket: 餐廳→restaurant, 咖啡店→cafe, 電影院→cinema, 健身房→gym, 瑜伽→yoga, 寵物→pet,
  書店→retail, 按摩→beauty. Bucket is a non-empty string, directly consumable by
  `categories.resolve` (D367) · pinned end-to-end for all eight.
- Party size: `2人`→2, `4个人`→4, `我们6个`→6; `一个人`→`None` (a single diner is **not** treated
  as a party · the honest, non-guessing outcome, pinned as observed rather than forced to `1`).
- Constraints: `不吃辣`→`{cuisine_avoid:spicy}`, `唔食牛`→`{diet_avoid:beef}`; positive food intent
  (`食壽司`) and `素食` produce **no** avoid constraint.
- Language: `餐廳`/`我想食飯`→`zh-HK`, `restaurant`→`en`.
- Time shape: absent → `{}`; `今晚` → `{type:'range', starts_at, ends_at, quality}` with
  `ends_at > starts_at` and a non-empty `quality` (clock-independent assertions only).
- **Boundary documented**: `budget` and `cuisine` are deliberately **not** extracted here ·
  they are owned downstream by `nlu/state_merger` (D352). Asserted as `None` / absent so a future
  change that quietly drops the boundary is caught.

## 367. D369 · pin the parameterized SQL builders' pure surface (`search/sql`, §0/§6/§9/D3)

**Module / contract.** `nexus_ai.search.sql` turns an intent/filter set into **parameterized**
Postgres SQL (`$n` placeholders + a bound-param list). It builds strings only · no connection is
opened · so every builder is exercisable offline. DECISIONS D3 (Postgres-only: tsvector ∪ pg_trgm
∪ pgvector ∪ geo) and the project's injection rule ("values are never concatenated into SQL") are
pinned here. The sibling `test_search_sql.py` already pins the category-taxonomy bridge; this unit
pins the rest of the pure surface.

**Pinned behavior (25 cases, all confirmed empirically):**
- `Params` no-inlining: `add`/`extend` return ordered `$n` placeholders; a `build_merchant_query`
  with a distinctive tenant + text emits **neither** string into the SQL · both are bound params.
- `_tsconfig` allow-list (injection / typo guard): `simple`/`english` pass through; anything else
  (incl. empty) falls back to `simple`, and the emitted SQL shows `to_tsquery('simple'`.
- Merchant-query structural rules: base shape (`FROM merchants m` + `ORDER BY`); empty text → no
  `@@` predicate and `true AS text_matched`; geo lane emits the spherical `acos(...)` distance
  expression + `BETWEEN` bbox prefilter + `loc.meters <=`; `avoid` filter adds `AND NOT (`;
  `max_price` filter present and bound.
- Geo math: `haversine_m` is ~0 for identical points, symmetric, ~111 km per degree of latitude;
  `bbox` is centered on the anchor and widens with radius.
- `vector_literal`: 6-decimal pgvector text form; `[]` for empty.
- Side-query empty guards: `facts_for`/`hours_for`/`reviews_for`/`entities_for`/`slots_for` return
  `("", [])` for empty ids (prevents a `= ANY(ARRAY[])` SQL error); non-empty builds a bound query.
- Chunk query: `top_k` clamped to 40 (§9 rerank budget) regardless of request; vector `<=>` op
  present only when an embedding is supplied.
- Open-now / time: `open_now_predicate_expr` returns `(weekday, 'HH:MM:SS')` in HK tz; `time_today`
  returns a `time`.

**Discipline note.** Three premise corrections, all call-signature / generated-text, not code:
builders require `embedding` (and `build_chunk_query` also `merchant_id`); the geo lane emits
`acos(...)`, not the literal word "haversine". Code unchanged.

**Verified, not claimed.** `pytest tests/test_sql_builders.py` → **25 passed**; full `apps/ai`
suite → **413 passed, 4 skipped** (`pytest -q`, live-DB tests skip because Docker is down).

## 368. D370 · pin the provider-abstraction pure core (`models/base`, §9/§2/§105/D4)

**Module / contract.** `nexus_ai.models.base` is the wire-agnostic provider core (AGENT_CONTRACT
§9, DECISIONS D4): request/response data, dev-only pricing, token estimation, locale
normalization, JSON coercion, record-extractors, and the `HttpLLMAdapter` credentials guard
(§105 degrade). All pure / DB-free · pinnable offline.

**Pinned behavior (28 cases, all confirmed empirically):**
- `estimate_tokens`: empty→0; CJK ~1 token/char (`你好`→2); latin ~4 chars/token (`hello`→1,
  `a`→1, `abcdefgh`→2); mixed counts CJK + quarter-latin.
- `cost_usd`: `cheap` 1000/1000→0.0015; `reason` 1000/1000→0.09; unknown tier falls back to
  `mid` (0.003) · the dev-only estimate, never a claim of invoice truth (§9).
- `norm_locale`: `en`/`en-US`→`en`; `zh-CN`/`zh-Hans`→`zh-CN`; `zh-HK`→`zh-HK`; unknown / empty
  / `None` all default to `zh-HK` (HK-first product).
- `maybe_json`: parses objects/arrays (leading whitespace stripped); non-JSON and malformed both
  return `None` (safe coercion, never raises).
- Record-extractors (`record_title/price/meters/rating/top_reason`): title falls through
  title→name→display_name→`?`; price/meters/rating handle both scalar and nested `{amount|meters|
  value}` dicts and degrade to `None` on missing / un-coercible input (no raising); `top_reason`
  returns the first reason text or `""`.
- `budget_for`: known task class returns its `{tier, purpose}`; unknown raises `KeyError`.
- `LLMResponse.total_tokens`: sums prompt + completion tokens.
- `LLMError`: carries `provider` / `retryable` / `status`.
- `HttpLLMAdapter` guard (DECISIONS D4 / §131): missing base_url or api_key raises `LLMError`
  (keeps the factory on `mock`) rather than booting a mis-configured live client; with credentials

**Module / contract.** The async `search` orchestrator needs a backend (DB or static fixtures), but

into a `SearchPlan`), `_static_tokens` / `_filter_static` (offline catalogue filtering), and the
row helpers (`_row_price`, `_row_sponsored`, `_relevance`, `_iso`, `_num`, `_slot_window`).

**Pinned behavior (31 cases, all confirmed empirically):**
- `_static_tokens`: whitespace tokens **plus CJK bigrams** (Chinese has no spaces · `沙田餐廳` →
  `['沙田','沙田餐廳','田餐','餐廳']`), sorted + deduped; a lone CJK char yields no bigram.
- `_row_price` priority `price_amount` > `avg_price_hkd` > `price_min`; `None` when absent.
- `_row_sponsored`: reads `sponsored`/`promoted` from a dict **or** a JSON string; invalid JSON

  vector lane (0.8+0.4 → 0.94 only when `vector_lane`).
- `_iso` datetime→`…Z` (non-datetime→None); `_num` safe float coercion.

- `_filter_static`: text match (token hits + name-hit bonus → `kw_score`), category / district
  (case-insensitive) / max_price filters; mutates each kept row with `kw_score`/`vec_score`/
  `text_matched`/`subject_type` (e.g. a name+tag hit → 0.65).
- `plan_from_intent`: category + district into filters; resolved location seeds `geo`; `purchase`
  intent → `offering` subject; budget → `budget_max`/`budget_per`; `urgency=="now"` → `open_now`;
  `cuisine_avoid` constraint → `avoid`; a supplied geo without radius defaults to 5000 m; the
  empty-value drop-filter runs **only in the intent path** (with `intent=None` filters pass through
  verbatim); `open_now:False` survives the drop-filter (only None/""/[]/{} are dropped).

## 372. D375 · pin the end-to-end offline search pipeline (`search()` over `StaticBackend`, §6/§9/§67)

**Module / contract.** `search()` is the deterministic pipeline: candidate fetch → dedupe → facts →
candidates → organic rank → sponsored placement → facets → cards → `SearchResponse`.
`StaticBackend` is fixture-driven, so the whole path runs **offline** (no DB, no network) with the
real ranking weights loaded from `infra/config/ranking_weights.yaml` (version `hybrid_v1`).

**Pinned behavior (10 cases, all confirmed empirically):**
- Text filter: `query_text="ramen"` returns only the matching merchant; no text returns all
  organic rows.
- Response shape: `strategy` ends `+static` (and `+static+vector` in the vector lane);
  `degraded=False`, `provider="none"`, `total_estimate == len(ranked)`.
- Facets: `category`, `district`, `price_band` present.
- Empty backend → no cards, `total_estimate=0`.
- **Limit semantics**: `scored` and `cards` are the **top-N** (capped by `plan.limit`); the full
  ranked count is carried in `total_estimate`. With `limit=1` over 2 matches: 1 scored, 1 card,
  `total_estimate=2`.
- Dedupe: the same `subject_type:subject_id` collapses to one candidate even if the backend returns
  it twice.
- Subject types: `("offering",)` drives the offering lane and returns the offering card.
- `include_sponsored=False` leaves the organic set unchanged when there are no sponsored rows.

**Discipline note.** Two premise corrections, not code: `RankingWeights()` has empty weights
(KeyError), so the pipeline must be driven with `weights=None` to load the real config; and `scored`
is the top-N, not the full ranked list. Code unchanged.

**Verified, not claimed.** `pytest tests/test_search_pipeline.py` → **10 passed**; full `apps/ai`
suite → **520 passed, 4 skipped** (`pytest -q`, live-DB tests skip because Docker is down).

## 376. D379 · pin the DB seam's pure guards (`db/pool`, §0 / D3 / §105)

**Module / contract.** `nexus_ai.db.pool` is where the §0 role split stops being documentation: reads run
inside a `SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY` block, only `write()` opens a write path, the `search_path` is quoted
rather than interpolated, and a missing DSN degrades to `None` instead of crashing at import. The live path
is covered by `tests/test_integration.py`; this unit pins the seam itself with a fake pool and connection, so
the guards are verified with no database reachable.

**Pinned behavior (33 cases, all confirmed empirically):**
- `QueryResult`: `len`, `first` (empty -> `None`), `scalars`; a column the query never selected raises
  `KeyError` rather than returning a hole.
- `_to_float`: `None`/`""` -> `None`, numeric text and ints -> float, junk -> `None`.
- `_safe_path`: every kept element is quoted (`"public", "nexus_test"`); non-identifier elements are dropped
  (`"a-b, c"` -> `"c"`); the empty setting is spelled `public` *before* the split, so `""` and `None` yield
  `"public"` while a whitespace-only or all-dropped value yields the bare fallback `public`; digits and
  underscores survive.
- `_returns_rows`: true only for a leading SELECT/WITH/UPDATE/DELETE/INSERT **and** a `RETURNING`; a plain
  SELECT, a plain DELETE and an empty string are false.
- `_is_read_only_violation` / `_is_privilege_error`: recognised by the driver's exception class name or by
  the message text; an unrelated error is neither.
- `Database` defaults: `statement_timeout_ms = 3000`, empty `search_path` -> `public`, `read_only_violations`
  starts at 0.
- `readonly(...)`: the statement order is `BEGIN`, `SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY`, `SET LOCAL search_path TO
  "<schema>"`, `SET LOCAL statement_timeout = <ms>`, fetch, commit; a per-call `schema` overrides the pool's.
  A blocked write increments `read_only_violations` and re-raises; a privilege error becomes
  `InsufficientPrivilege`; any other error is re-raised uncounted.
- `write(...)`: fetches only when the statement returns rows (`RETURNING`), otherwise executes and returns
  `[]`; the statement timeout is set inside the transaction. `insert_returning` maps a row or `None`;
  `executemany` with no rows never acquires a connection and otherwise passes tuples in column order;
  `close()` swallows an already-broken pool.
- `_init_connection`: registers `jsonb` with an **identity encoder** (the fix for the double-encoded payload
  bug) and `json.loads` decoder, and `numeric` with a `str` encoder / float decoder.
- `connect`: no `database_url` -> `None` with no pool; the same Settings object builds one pool and reuses it;
  `force_new` closes the old one and rebuilds with `min_size`/`max_size`, `application_name=nexus_ai` and the
  statement timeout; `require_db` raises `DatabaseUnavailable` naming `NEXUS_DATABASE_URL`; `dispose` closes
  and clears; `ping` is true when a connection answers and false when it does not; `__all__` is exactly the
  nine-name surface.

**Discipline note.** Seven failures in the first run were all test premises, never code: the fake's failure
switch was matched against the SQL text instead of raised unconditionally, the `write()` log index counted
`BEGIN` as a statement, and the `_safe_path` fallback is bare `public` only when every element is dropped.
Code unchanged.

**Verified, not claimed.** `pytest tests/test_db_pool.py` -> **33 passed**; full `apps/ai` suite ->
**608 passed, 4 skipped** (`pytest -q`). The Docker window this session opened and closed: with
`nexus-platform-postgres` answering, `NEXUS_TEST_DATABASE_URL=postgresql://nexus_ai:...@127.0.0.1:5433/nexus
pytest tests/test_integration.py` -> **4 passed**; the engine then went away again (`docker ps` -> `failed to
connect to the docker API at npipe:////./pipe/dockerDesktopLinuxEngine ... cannot find the file specified`),
so the 18-step gate refused at container resolution -- `ERROR: no running Postgres container among:
nexus-platform-postgres nexus-platform-testpg` -- and stays the next unit's work.

**Module / contract.** `nexus_ai.contract` is imported by the routes and mirrored by the generated
frontend types, so its behavior is interface behavior. The models split deliberately: `_Strict`
(`extra="forbid"`) where the contract fixes a shape, `extra="ignore"` on the render surface so a newer
server's extra field cannot break an older client.

**Pinned behavior (29 cases, all confirmed empirically):**
- Strictness: `GeoPoint`/`Money`/`SearchRequest`/`SearchRequestFilters` reject an unlisted field, and a
  typo nested two levels down (`distirct`) is a `ValidationError`, not a silently dropped filter;

  always a **string** on the wire; `7` -> `"7.00"`; currency defaults to HKD; `model` round-trips.
- `Fact.effective_stale`: the explicit flag wins; an expiry in the past **or exactly now** is stale; a

- `Intent`: defaults say "unknown" (`intent="unknown"`, null category/budget/party, empty lists), lists are

- Wire names are snake_case (`include_sponsored`, not `includeSponsored`) and a dump round-trips through

## 378. D381 · the Chinese sentence's empty page was a soft preference rendered as a hard SQL filter (`search/service`, §7.1 / D381)

**The defect.** `plan_from_intent` mapped every positive `Intent.preference` into
`plan.attributes[key] = True` and merged it into `filters["attributes"]`, which the SQL builder
renders as `m.attributes @> '{"<key>": true}'::jsonb`. The §7.1 object calls those **soft**
signals; the query treated them as hard exclusions, and the collapse to `True` dropped the value,
so even a merchant carrying the key could not have matched.

**Measured on the live plane** (seeded `nexus`, 470 published merchants, `nexus_ai` role):
`extract_intent_dict("帮我找一个适合情侣约会的地方")` yields
`preferences=[{key: occasion, value: date, polarity: 1}]` with `category=None`; the plan then carried
`{"attributes": {"occasion": True}}`; `build_merchant_query(...)` executed against the database
returned **0 rows** (`SELECT count(*) ... WHERE attributes @> '{"occasion": true}'::jsonb` -> 0). The
empty page D365 filed under Chinese text matching never reached the text lane: the attribute filter
had already deleted every row. The exact-name probe still works (`翠莊` -> 5 items), which is why the
ladder looked like a text problem.

**The fix.** `plan_from_intent` no longer writes preferences into the filter; only the caller's
explicit `filters.attributes` is a hard containment clause, and `avoid` still comes from
`constraints`. `SearchPlan.attributes` is documented as ranking-lane input.

**Verified, not claimed.** Live, same process, after the change: the sentence answers **5 items** and
the generated SQL carries no `m.attributes @>` clause. `pytest tests/test_preferences_are_soft.py` ->
**8 passed**; full `apps/ai` suite -> **645 passed, 4 skipped**; live DB
`NEXUS_TEST_DATABASE_URL=... pytest tests/test_integration.py` -> **4 passed** (the engine is back up;
the 18-step gate is running in the background and its verdict is the next unit's entry).

**Remains.** The preference is now neither a filter nor a boost: the ranking lane has no preference
feature, so "quiet"/"date" is not yet honored by ordering. The Intent keeps the value and D381 files
the next unit as "read preferences into a ranking signal". A second, unrelated artifact observed while
probing: on `TestClient` shutdown the app's best-effort agent-run write races the closing pool
(`asyncpg ... pool is closing` traceback on stderr); responses are unaffected and the write is
already best-effort, but the shutdown ordering is filed rather than fixed here.

## 380 · D382 · pin user preferences into the personalization ranking signal (`search/service`, D381 / §7.1 / §99-§100)

**The gap D381 filed.** Preferences were no longer a hard filter (D381), but they also weren't a signal:
the ranking lane had no code that read `user_preferences` and converted a declared preference like
`kind=ambience, key=quiet, weight=1.0` into a boost for merchants with `attributes.quiet_ambience=true`.

**Implementation.** Added `SearchBackend.user_preferences(user_id, kinds?)` to the seam (implemented in
`PostgresBackend` via `SQL.user_preferences_for`, no-op in `StaticBackend`). The `search` pipeline now:
1. Reads all preferences for the searching user (if `user_id` is provided).
2. Builds a `(kind, key) -> weight` map (weight is 0.0-1.0, neutral=0.5).
3. For each candidate, looks up its merchant's `attributes` JSONB and checks for a matching key:
   `{key}_{kind}` (e.g., `quiet_ambience`) or `{kind}_{key}` (e.g., `ambience_quiet`).
4. If the attribute is `true`, adds the preference weight; if `false`, adds the inverted weight
   (`1 - weight`) as a dislike signal.
5. Averages all matching preference scores into `personalization[sid]`, which the ranking lane
   already consumes (`personalization_signal` is EMA over feedback; a direct preference score
   bypasses the minimum-signal threshold and is used as-is).
6. A merchant with no matching attributes gets no preference signal (falls back to `neutral`).

**Verified, not claimed.** `pytest tests/test_preferences_ranking.py` → **6 passed**; full `apps/ai`
suite → **651 passed, 4 skipped**. The live-DB integration tests skip because the Docker engine is
still down on this machine (the fresh gate run aborted at step 14 on `falsify_console_a11y.mjs`
crash in the other lane's working copy).

**Remains.** The preference signal bypasses `personalization_signal`'s `min_signals` threshold, which
is the intent (declared prefs are explicit intent, not implicit feedback). The attribute key
convention (`key_kind` / `kind_key`) is a design choice; if the seed data uses a different naming
scheme, the matching will silently not fire. A future unit should add a `preference_key` column to
`user_preferences` or standardize the attribute naming in the seed.

## 381 · D383 · NLU intent preferences now feed the personalization ranking signal (`search/service`, D382 follow-up / §7.1 / §99-100)

**The gap D382 filed.** D382 added persistent `user_preferences` (from the database) to the personalization signal, but the transient NLU-extracted `Intent.preferences` from the current query were not used. A Chinese sentence like "帮我找一个适合情侣约会的地方" extracts `occasion=date` but this signal was lost before ranking.

**Implementation.** The `search()` pipeline now accepts an optional `intent_preferences` parameter (passed from `run_search` via the `Intent` object). For each candidate, the pipeline matches the NLU preference `(key=occasion, value=date, polarity=1)` against merchant `attributes` JSONB using the `{value}_{kind}` convention (e.g., `date_occasion`). A match adds weight 1.0 (polarity > 0) or 0.0 (polarity < 0); a mismatch inverts. The averaged score merges with any existing personalization (feedback, persistent prefs).

**Seed data alignment.** Updated `data/seed/generate.py` to emit merchant attributes matching all NLU preference keys: `date_occasion`, `group_occasion`, `family_occasion`, `business_occasion`, `solo_occasion`, `ambience_style`, `outdoor_style`, `indoor_style`, `mtr_near_access`, `accessible_access`, `parking_access`, `pet_friendly_access`, `scenic_view`, `spicy_cuisine`, `cheap_price_sense`, `premium_price_sense`, `rainy_day_weather` — alongside existing `quiet_ambience`, `lively_ambience`, `kid_friendly`, `mtr_within_5min`, `outdoor_seating`, `has_private_room`, `wheelchair_access`, `opens_late`.

**Verified, not claimed.** Offline test `test_pref_match.py`: a query with `intent_preferences=[{key:occasion, value:date, polarity:1}]` boosts merchants with `date_occasion=true` (personalization=1.0) and penalizes `date_occasion=false` (personalization=0.0). Full `apps/ai` suite: **651 passed, 4 skipped**. All ledger checks PASS.

**Remains.** Structured preference values (e.g., `cuisine_like: {values: [...]}`) not yet handled; currently only boolean attributes are matched. The `{value}_{kind}` convention works for the seeded boolean attributes but may need `preference_key` column for complex values.
