## 510. D516 · the search's `filters.tags` did not speak the spelling the `tags` COLUMN is written in (`apps/ai/nexus_ai/search/categories.py`, `apps/ai/nexus_ai/search/service.py`, `apps/ai/tests/test_the_filter_speaks_the_tags_vocabulary.py`, `apps/ai/tests/test_live_search_contract.py`)

**What was measured.** `search/sql.py:164` turns `filters.tags` into `m.tags && ARRAY[...]` - an
exact array overlap against a column the seed writes. The seed writes every tag as a lowercase
hyphen slug: measured against the live corpus, `select distinct unnest(tags) from merchants`
returns 100 tags and every one matches `^[a-z0-9-]+$`. The filter, however, passed the caller's
raw string straight through, so a caller who spelled a tag the way the product spells it in
prose matched NOTHING:

    filters {"tags": ["cantonese"]}      -> 11 rows
    filters {"tags": ["Cantonese"]}      -> 0 rows
    filters {"tags": ["escape_room"]}    -> 0 rows   ("escape-room" -> 6)
    filters {"tags": ["  cantonese  "]}  -> 0 rows

the D505/D508 lesson in a third place: the same fact (how a tag is spelled) had two readers,
and one of them was the raw string. Two further defects rode along in the same lane. The
`plan_from_intent` intent-None branch returned early before any normalisation, so the
filter-only caller got nothing normalised at all - category and district were read there,
tags were not. And `_canonical_tags` iterated `filters["tags"]` directly, so a caller passing
one tag as a bare string (`{"tags": "ramen"}`) handed the predicate five tags, none of which
any merchant carries.

**The fix.** One reader, exported and shared: `categories.canonical_tag` case-folds, trims and
hyphenates through the module's own `_slug`, the same separator rule that already folds a
category bucket into the taxonomy's spelling (`escape_room` -> `escape-room`). `_slug` now
covers whitespace as well as `_`, which is what makes `escape room` and `escape_room` one
word. `_canonical_tags` routes every tag through it on BOTH branches of `plan_from_intent`,
and wraps a lone string into a one-element list before iterating. The reader RESPELLS and
never REWORDS - no alias table, no lexicon - so a tag the product does not know keeps its
word and still matches nothing, rather than being resolved into a tag the caller never asked
for. This also retires the sibling lane's D509 WIP, which was in the tree as a no-op: its
if/else both appended the tag unchanged, it was called only on the intent branch, and its
companion gate asserted the pass-through it was meant to replace (and was the one red
`ruff check .` at HEAD). The gate is now a real one.

**Discipline note.** Three readers of one fact in one lane - the seed's slug rule, the SQL
`&&`, and the caller's raw string - is the D488 shape again, and the fix is the same shape
too: not a second normaliser next to the first, but the first one, exported and called from
the place that was guessing. The "respells, never rewords" invariant is what keeps the fix
from becoming an alias table by accident; it is stated as an independent restatement of the
lexicon's own word-identity rule rather than by calling the code under test.

**Verified, not claimed.** The tags vocabulary gate: **50 passed** (31 fixed-point/idempotence
checks over tags measured from the live corpus, 5 spelling families, 5 reword refusals, both
branches of the plan reader, the lone-string case, the empty-list case). Proved to fail:
disabling the reader reddens **12** of them (`test_every_spelling_of_a_stored_tag_reaches_the
stored_tag` x5, `test_both_branches_of_the_plan_reader_read_the_tags` x5,
`test_a_lone_string_is_one_tag_not_one_tag_per_character`, `test_an_unknown_tag_keeps_its_
word`) - the probe was put back and the suite returned to green. Two live-contract tests
added and proved the same way: `cantonese` and `Cantonese` now return the SAME cards on both
the intent-None and the intent path, against the live database. Targeted regression
(search plan, categories, search sql, search pipeline, both vocabulary gates, live contract,
cuisine vocabulary, understand resolution) -> **246 passed**; `mypy nexus_ai` -> **Success:
no issues found in 59 source files**; `ruff check .` -> **All checks passed** (it was red at
HEAD on the sibling's in-flight file); eval gate -> **PASS - 2 suite(s), 0 failing**; the ten
CI checkers -> green, and line-cite-drift re-measured at **116/176** citations still naming
the line they were written against (strict=none).
## 511. D517 · the search's `avoid` filter spoke a vocabulary the corpus does not have, and the planner threw the caller's own list away (`apps/ai/nexus_ai/search/categories.py`, `apps/ai/nexus_ai/search/service.py`, `apps/ai/nexus_ai/search/sql.py`, `apps/ai/tests/test_the_filter_speaks_the_avoid_vocabulary.py`, `apps/ai/tests/test_live_search_contract.py`)

**What was measured.** Two defects in one lane, both the D488 shape - the same fact read by two
readers, one of them the raw string.

The first is in the planner. `plan_from_intent` ended with `out["avoid"] = plan.avoid`, and
`plan.avoid` holds only what the INTENT's constraints named. So a caller who sent
`{"avoid": ["pork"]}` alongside an intent that named nothing had their hard filter overwritten
by an empty list - and the empty-filter sweep on the next line then dropped the key
altogether. Measured: `plan.filters` carried no `avoid` at all. §7.1 says the request's filters
are HARD, so a caller who asked to avoid pork was not filtered.

The second is in the SQL. The avoid clause compared the canonical constraint token to
`m.category_primary` with `=` and to the offering names with ILIKE. The taxonomy's leaf for the
same word is `seafood-grill`, and the column stores the leaf's NAME ("Seafood & BBQ"), so the
`=` leg could never fire and the ILIKE leg saw only the prose. Measured on the live corpus:
`avoid=["seafood"]` removed 16 of the 470 published merchants, and all 14 published merchants
tagged `seafood-grill` survived it. The tags column - the one place the corpus records the
fact - was never read.

**The fix.** One reader, exported and shared: `categories.avoid_terms` folds the value through
the lexin's OWN cuisine bridge (`cuisine_leaves`, D394) - the same reader the preference lane
reads a cuisine with - and offers the bridge all three spellings of the word (`dim_sum`,
`dim-sum`, `dim sum`), because the bridge is keyed on the intent vocabulary's underscore form
while the corpus writes the hyphenated slug. `search/sql.py` binds that term set in both lanes
and reads `m.tags &&` alongside the category and the offering names, so the two lanes exclude
the same merchants for the same word. The planner now merges the caller's explicit list with
the intent's constraints, deduped and order-stable, instead of overwriting one with the other.
Measured after: `avoid=["seafood"]` removes 30 of the 470 published merchants and excludes
every one of the 14 published `seafood-grill` merchants; through the API, a `seafood` query at
limit 50 loses 19 merchants to the filter.

**Discipline note.** The avoid filter and the preference lane were two readers of one fact, and
the avoid one was reading a vocabulary no table in this corpus speaks - it compared a
lowercase ascii token to a column of display names. That is why it was invisible: the clause
was never empty, it just never matched anything it was written to match. Re-aiming it through
the lexin's existing bridge rather than adding a second table is what keeps the two lanes from
drifting apart again, and the gate asserts the equivalence directly (the term set the SQL binds
must contain every leaf the bridge names) instead of trusting the reader.

**Verified, not claimed.** The vocabulary gate: **35 passed** (every `CUISINE_LEAVES` key
reaches its leaves through every spelling, the two SQL lanes bind the same term set, the
caller's list survives the intent path, the merge is deduped and order-stable). Proved to fail
in both halves separately: reverting the SQL expansion reddens the two lane checks; reverting
the planner merge reddens the three planner checks; reverting both reddens the two new
live-contract tests. Live contract: **10 passed** - `avoid=["seafood"]` now serves none of the
14 published `seafood-grill` merchants, and the caller's own list measurably changes the answer
(19 of 50 cards). Targeted regression (avoid gate, tags gate, live contract, sql builders,
search plan, preferences-are-soft, categories, search pipeline, constraint vocabulary, state
merger, understand resolution, cuisine vocabulary) -> **261 passed**; `mypy nexus_ai` ->
**Success: no issues found in 59 source files**; `ruff check .` -> **All checks passed**; eval
gate -> **PASS - 2 suite(s), 0 failing**; the ten CI checkers -> green, and line-cite-drift
re-measured at **117/177** citations still naming the line they were written against
(strict=none). §510's citation of `search/sql.py` line 131 was re-aimed to `:146`, because this unit's
own insertion moved it.
## 512. D518 · the party size had two readers, and the merge's copy invented a number the first turn refused to (`apps/ai/nexus_ai/nlu/understand.py`, `apps/ai/nexus_ai/nlu/state_merger.py`, `apps/ai/tests/test_the_party_size_has_one_reader.py`)

**What was measured.** `state_merger.py` carried a comment that said the merge reads the party
size with "the shared reader ... in `nlu/understand`". It did not. It kept a private copy of
the pattern, and the copy had lost the leading-digit guard `PARTY_RE` puts on its CJK
alternative (`(?:\D|^)`), so a digit run that is part of a LONGER number was read as a party
size. Measured at HEAD, with a non-cold-start base so the follow-up branch runs:

    "113個人"   -> the first turn reads NO party size (§8: do not invent a number)
                -> the merge read THIRTEEN SEATS
    "113位"     -> None  /  13
    "HK$113位人" -> None  /  13
    "這角落有213人" -> None  /  13

One fact, two readers, and the merge's copy was the one that invented a number. Every form the
product's own tables name agreed - the spelled-out Chinese numerals (三個人, 十一個人, 兩個人),
the latin units (guests, diners, persons, pax, "party of 4", "for 6 people") - so the drift
was confined to the long digit runs, which is exactly the kind of gap a private copy hides.

**The fix.** `understand.party_size_of` is now the ONE reader: it runs `PARTY_RE` over
`party_text(text)` and applies the 1..40 range, which is what `_fill_party` was already doing
inline. `_fill_party` calls it, and `merge_turn` calls it too, so the merge's private regex is
gone. The reader is exported rather than private because the whole point is that the second
turn imports the first turn's rule instead of restating it.

**Discipline note.** This is the D476/D487 shape arriving a third time: a comment asserted a
shared reader, the code kept a copy, and the copy drifted in the one direction that matters -
it read MORE than the guarded original. A comment is not a coupling; the import is. The gate
therefore asserts the coupling structurally (the merge's source must name the shared reader)
as well as behaviourally, because a behavioural gate alone passes the moment someone re-copies
the pattern with the cases they remember.

**Verified, not claimed.** The gate: **67 passed** - 12 forms the product's tables name read
identically by both turns, 10 turns that must not be read at all read by neither, the
structural coupling check, and the guard pinned on its own. Proved to fail: putting the
private copy back reddens **5** of them (the four long-digit-run refusals and the structural
check) - the probe was put back and the suite returned to green. Targeted regression (party
gate, state merger, search plan, understand resolution, sql builders, categories, the two
vocabulary gates, the two-readers-agree gate, merge cue spellings, negations, cuisine
vocabulary) -> **367 passed**; `mypy nexus_ai` -> **Success: no issues found in 59 source
files**; `ruff check .` -> **All checks passed**; eval gate -> **PASS - 2 suite(s), 0
failing**; the ten CI checkers -> green.
## 513. D519 · the district reader could not read the spelling the corpus writes its districts in - and four of the corpus's fifteen districts were missing from it entirely (`apps/ai/nexus_ai/nlu/lexicon.py`, `apps/ai/tests/test_the_district_speaks_the_corpus_spelling.py`)

**What was measured.** A district has three spellings in this product: the DISPLAY NAME
("Sha Tin", which `locations.district` holds and the SQL compares), the SPACED form ("sha
tin", which the lexin's alias table carries), and the SLUG (`sha-tin`, which the seed writes
as a tag on every merchant in the district). `match_district` compares its aliases LITERALLY
through `cue_in`, and the alias table only had the spaced form - so the corpus's own spelling
resolved to nothing. Measured on the live corpus: of the 15 district tags the seed writes,
**1** resolved (`central`, the only single-word one) and 14 did not. Through the API:

    filters={"district": "sha-tin"}  -> 0 items
    filters={"district": "Sha Tin"}  -> 50 items (the limit)

The second defect sat behind the first: the lexin's `DISTRICTS` held 20 districts and the
corpus writes 15 of them, but four were absent from the table altogether - Tai Wai (137
published merchants, the second-largest district in the corpus), Ma On Shan (50), Kowloon Bay
(14) and Stanley (6). A user who asked for any of them got no district and no geo anchor.

**The fix.** Two halves, one theme. `_hyphenate_district_aliases` runs after the vocabulary
canonicalisation and adds the folded form of every Latin district name and alias to that
district's alias list - folded by the product's ONE separator rule
(`categories.canonical_tag`, the same rule that folds a category bucket and a tag), not a
second one. And the four missing districts are added from the seed's own DISTRICTS table,
which is the writer of both `locations.district` and the district tags - so the coordinates
are the seed's, not an estimate. The table now holds 24 districts and every one of the 15
corpus district tags resolves: `sha-tin` -> Sha Tin, `tai-wai` -> Tai Wai,
`ma-on-shan` -> Ma On Shan, `kowloon-bay` -> Kowloon Bay, `stanley` -> Stanley.

**Discipline note.** The alias table was not wrong so much as incomplete in a direction
nobody looked: every alias a human would type was there, and the one spelling the corpus
itself writes was not. That is the D516 shape again - the writer and the reader of one fact
disagreeing about a separator - and the fix is the same shape too: fold with the rule the
product already has, and take the missing rows from the writer rather than inventing them.
The gate pins the coupling (the folded spelling must be IN the table, so a district added
later inherits the fold) as well as the behaviour, because a behavioural gate alone would
pass the moment someone adds a district and forgets its hyphen.

**Verified, not claimed.** The gate: **79 passed** - all 15 corpus district tags resolve to
the district the corpus says they are and filter to it through `plan_from_intent`, every
Latin spelling of every district in the table resolves, the folded spelling is in the table,
and the display name and spaced form still resolve (the fold adds, never replaces). Proved to
fail in both halves separately: removing the fold reddens **46** checks; removing the four
districts reddens **8**. Live contract re-measured: `kowloon-bay` -> 14 items and `stanley`
-> 6 items, exactly the published-merchant counts the corpus holds. Targeted regression
(district spelling gate, district vocabulary gate, lexicon, canonical forms, lexicon readers,
vocabulary code points, search plan, understand resolution, state merger, sql builders) ->
**538 passed**, and (live contract, live sort preference, search pipeline, preferences are
soft, the tags gate, the avoid gate, the party-size gate) -> **182 passed**; `mypy nexus_ai`
-> **Success: no issues found in 59 source files**; `ruff check .` -> **All checks passed**;
eval gate -> **PASS - 2 suite(s), 0 failing**; the ten CI checkers -> green.

## 514. D520 · two test fixtures wrote a code point the product's vocabulary does not carry - and one of them was the base of another lane's gate (`apps/ai/tests/test_the_party_size_has_one_reader.py`, `apps/ai/tests/test_the_filter_speaks_the_avoid_vocabulary.py`)

**What was measured.** The D453 gate derives its reference from the product's own package -
every Chinese character the package carries, its data and not its prose - and then reads every
string constant in `tests/`. A character neither the product nor the `DECLARED` list knows is a
word the platform has never heard of. Running the targeted regression for the next unit turned
it RED on `U+63C4`, in two files: the D518 party-size gate's `BASE` state and the D517 avoid
gate's `_intent()` base - both `"揄餐廳"`, where the Cantonese "find a restaurant"
(`搵餐廳`, which `DISCOVER_CUES` carries) was meant. One of the two wrote the
character literally and the other wrote it as a `\u63c4` escape, so a reader grepping for the
glyph found only one of them.

**The fix.** Both spellings of the same word, corrected to the character the vocabulary
carries. In the avoid gate this is not only a cosmetic repair: `_intent()` builds its base with
`extract_intent_dict`, and the unintelligible query made that base `intent="unknown"` with
`category=None` - so D517's planner gate had been measuring the intent path with an intent
that named nothing. With the word the product knows, the same assertions pass on a base that
is a real `discover_merchant` / `restaurant`.

**Discipline note.** D517 and D518 were committed with this red and nobody saw it, because
each unit ran the tests it had written rather than the gate that reads the test FILES. The
code-point gate is the one that reads what a test file SAYS rather than what it asserts, and
it is the only thing that would have caught it. A red gate found while validating the next
unit is a defect of this unit, not a note in the next one's entry.

**Verified, not claimed.** The gate was red on exactly this character before the fix and green
after (proved to fail by the measurement itself). Targeted regression (cuisine, lexicon,
polarity, intent, vocabulary, canonical, party size, avoid) -> **1234 passed**; live (search
contract, live preferences, live vocabulary spelling, live conversation refinement) -> **22
passed**; `mypy nexus_ai` -> **Success: no issues found in 59 source files**; `ruff check .`
-> **All checks passed**; eval gate -> **PASS - 2 suite(s), 0 failing**; the ten CI checkers
-> green.

## 515. D521 · the cuisine row that could not read its own name (`apps/ai/nexus_ai/nlu/lexicon.py`, `apps/ai/tests/test_the_cuisine_row_speaks_its_own_name.py`, `apps/ai/tests/test_live_search_contract.py`)

**What was measured.** The lexicon has eleven cuisine rows, and ten of them carry the cuisine's
OWN name among their terms: a user who types "italian", "korean", "thai", "seafood" or "dim
sum" gets the cuisine. The eleventh - `japanese` - does not. Its row is the Japanese words and
the transliterations and never the word itself, so the one word the product uses for the
cuisine in its own maps (`CUISINE_LEAVES`, `_CUISINE_CATEGORY_MAP`, the ranking labels) is the
one word its reader cannot read. Measured through the extractor:

    extract_intent("japanese")                     -> intent "unknown", category None, preferences []
    extract_intent("i want japanese")              -> intent "unknown"
    extract_intent("somewhere japanese in central") -> intent "unknown"

and through the API on the live corpus, `query="japanese"` was read as `intent: unknown` with
no category and no preference, and the 50 cards served to a user who asked for Japanese food
were a mixed bag - a nail salon, a phone repair shop, a swimming centre, a gym, a bookshop -
with exactly **1** of the corpus's 27 published Japanese-leaf merchants in them, at rank 9, by
accident of ranking rather than by any signal.

**The fix.** One term: `"japanese"` joins its own row. The same query now reads as
`discover_merchant` / `restaurant` with a `cuisine=japanese` preference, and the answer
carries **3** of the 27 (ranks 8, 32, 48).

**Discipline note.** The row was authored Chinese-first, and the English name of the one
cuisine whose English name is also the product's own word for it was the one left out. Ten
rows happen to carry their own name and one does not, and nothing held the eleven to the
rule - so the gate takes its parameter from the table (`sorted(CUISINE_TERMS)`) and folds the
separators, because the row key is `dim_sum` and the user writes "dim sum". A twelfth row
inherits the rule instead of relying on somebody remembering it.

**Verified, not claimed.** The gate: **17 passed** - every row reads its own name in the
spelling a user types it, and a query naming the cuisine is understood with a category and a
cuisine preference. Proved to fail: deleting the term from the row reddens every check here
(the probe was put back). Live contract re-measured on this database: `query="japanese"` ->
`discover_merchant` / `restaurant` with a `cuisine` preference, and the merchants the corpus
tags `sushi` / `ramen` / `izakaya` surface (**11 passed** in that file). Targeted regression
(cuisine, lexicon, polarity, intent, vocabulary, canonical forms) -> **1142 passed**; live
(search contract, preferences, vocabulary spelling, conversation refinement) -> **22 passed**;
`mypy nexus_ai` -> **Success: no issues found in 59 source files**; `ruff check .` -> **All
checks passed**; eval gate -> **PASS - 2 suite(s), 0 failing**; the ten CI checkers -> green.

## 516. D522 · the query's own cuisine preference was read out of a JSONB key the seed never writes - and a DISLIKE scored the maximum (`apps/ai/nexus_ai/search/service.py`, `apps/ai/tests/test_the_intent_cuisine_reads_the_rows_columns.py`, `apps/ai/tests/test_live_search_contract.py`)

**What was measured.** A merchant's `category_primary` and `tags` are COLUMNS on its row.
The `attributes` JSONB carries the booleans - `quiet_ambience`, `wheelchair_access`,
`opens_late` - and never the category, never the tags (measured on this corpus). The
stored-preference path knew that and folded the row's columns in before matching; the
transient path - the one that serves the preferences the user typed in THIS query - read
`attrs.get("category_primary")` and `attrs.get("tags")` straight out of the JSONB, so both
were empty for every merchant in the corpus. An empty category and an empty tag list never
match a cuisine, so every cuisine preference fell to the non-matching branch:

    a cuisine the user LIKED    -> 0.5
    a cuisine the user DISLIKED -> 1.0   (the maximum)

Measured through the API on the live corpus, `query="素食唔好"` (not vegetarian) gave
every Vegetarian merchant `personalization = 1.0` and they ranked **1, 2, 3, 4**, while
`query="想食素食"` (I want vegetarian) gave them `0.5`. The platform scored the thing
the user refused above the thing they asked for - and the card named no preference at all,
because a match that never fires records no label.

**The fix.** One reader of one fact: `_enriched_attrs(row, attrs)` folds the row's own
columns (`avg_price_hkd`, `district`, `category_primary`, `tags`) into the JSONB, and BOTH
preference paths now call it - the stored path's inline copy is gone. Measured after:
`想食素食` -> the Vegetarian merchants rank 1, 2, 3, 4;
`素食唔好` -> they fall to 21, 35, 43; `想食日料` -> Ramen & Noodles at 1, 2;
`唔好日料` -> no Japanese leaf in the top 50 at all.

**Discipline note.** The stored path had the enrichment inline and the transient path did
not, and the copy that drifted is the one that serves the live query - the D518 shape again,
one fact with two readers. D394's gate covered the stored path (`user_preferences`,
`cuisine_like`) and passed the whole time, because a gate written against one reader says
nothing about its twin. Folding the row's columns is now the ONE reader both paths call, so
the next preference kind cannot be added to one lane and forgotten in the other.

**Verified, not claimed.** The gate: **12 passed** - the query's cuisine fires on the
merchant the corpus tags (five spellings across five cuisines), the polarity points the
right way in both directions, the card names the preference as `typed`, and the intent block
is pinned to the shared reader. Proved to fail: reading `merchant_attrs[mid]` instead of
`_enriched_attrs(r, ...)` reddens **9** of the 12, and the live check with it. Live contract
re-measured on this database (**12 passed** in that file). Targeted regression (cuisine,
preference, personalization, ranking, search, intent, card) -> **806 passed**; live (search
contract, preferences, sort preference, vocabulary spelling, conversation refinement) ->
**25 passed**; `mypy nexus_ai` -> **Success: no issues found in 59 source files**; `ruff
check .` -> **All checks passed**; eval gate -> **PASS - 2 suite(s), 0 failing**; the ten CI
checkers -> green.

## 517. D523 · a negated cuisine was a LIKE, in Chinese as in English - the polarity reader was handed the wrong word (`apps/ai/nexus_ai/nlu/lexicon.py`, `apps/ai/nexus_ai/nlu/understand.py`, `apps/ai/tests/test_a_negated_cuisine_is_a_dislike.py`)

**What was measured.** `apply_polarity` re-stamps the polarity of EVERY preference on the
Intent, and its contract is explicit: `tokens` maps a preference's (key, value) to the
SURFACE term that matched it, "because the canonical value is not in a Chinese sentence,
but the token that matched is". The cuisine preferences are put on the Intent by
`_fill_category`, which appended them with no token at all - so the reader fell back to the
canonical value, and a Chinese sentence negating a cuisine carried none of it. Measured
before the fix, every one of these came back polarity **+1**:

    "素食唔好"             -> cuisine=vegetarian, polarity +1
    "唔好素食"             -> cuisine=vegetarian, polarity +1
    "不想吃海鲜"          -> cuisine=seafood,    polarity +1
    "不要日料"             -> cuisine=japanese,   polarity +1
    "食么都好 唔好日式" -> cuisine=japanese,   polarity +1

The English rows worked, and only by luck of the same fallback: "no seafood" happens to
carry the canonical value inside the sentence. Nothing was wrong with the polarity grammar -
the reader was being handed the wrong word.

**The fix.** `match_cuisine_terms` is the ONE cuisine matcher and returns
`(cuisine, the surface term that matched it)`; `match_cuisines` is now its projection, so
there is still one matcher and no second copy of the rule. `_fill_preferences` feeds those
terms into the token map it already hands `apply_polarity`, and the reader sees the word the
user actually typed. Measured after: every negation above reads -1, every affirmation reads
+1, and the ranking lane points the right way (a refusal now demotes the merchants that
carry the cuisine - see §516 for the measured ranking effect).

**Discipline note.** The bug was invisible in English and total in Chinese, which is the
same asymmetry D420 found in the locale detection: a reader that falls back to a canonical
value can only ever be right for the language the canonical value is written in. The gate
therefore takes its parameter from the table - every cuisine row, its own Chinese term,
negated before and after - rather than listing the sentences that happened to be measured.

**Verified, not claimed.** The gate: **35 passed** - every cuisine row's own term negated
reads -1 and affirmed reads +1, the English negations read -1, and the coupling is pinned
(the token map is built from `match_cuisine_terms`, and it still reaches `apply_polarity`).
Proved to fail: reverting `_fill_preferences` to build the token map from `PREFERENCE_RULES`
alone reddens **14** of the 35 (the probe was put back). Targeted regression (cuisine,
lexicon, polarity, intent, vocabulary, canonical forms, preference, merger, state) ->
**1512 passed**; live (search contract, preferences, conversation refinement) -> **22
passed**; `mypy nexus_ai` -> **Success: no issues found in 59 source files**; `ruff check .`
-> **All checks passed**; eval gate -> **PASS - 2 suite(s), 0 failing**; the ten CI checkers
-> green.

## 518. D524 · the category filter widened 21 of the taxonomy's 67 leaves into their whole root (`apps/ai/nexus_ai/search/service.py`, `apps/ai/nexus_ai/search/sql.py`, `apps/ai/tests/test_the_category_filter_keeps_the_leaf_the_caller_named.py`, `apps/ai/tests/test_live_search_contract.py`)

**What was measured.** `filters.category` is read by the SAME reader as the intent's category
(D505), and that reader answers with a coarse BUCKET. For 21 of the taxonomy's 67 leaves the
bucket is COARSER than what the caller wrote, because the leaf's own name contains a word
the reader also knows - "coffee" is a word inside `specialty-coffee`, "salon" inside
`hair-salon`, "bar" inside `cocktail-bar` (a hyphen is a word boundary, so the reader is
right to see the word). The leaf was rewritten into its root and the caller's HARD filter
(§7.1) silently became the whole root. Measured on the live corpus, `query=""` with

    filters={"category": "specialty-coffee"}  -> 79 merchants  (the corpus holds 33)
    filters={"category": "cocktail-bar"}      -> 39 merchants  (the corpus holds 13)
    filters={"category": "hair-salon"}        -> 39 merchants  (the corpus holds 11)

The other 46 leaves passed through untouched (`match_category` does not know their names),
which is what made the defect invisible: one fact, one filter, and an answer that depended
on whether the leaf's name happened to contain a category word.

**The fix.** The taxonomy is the only plane that knows which slugs are leaves, so the
caller's own spelling now travels beside the bucket (`category_spelling`, respelled by the
product's ONE separator rule) and the SQL asks the taxonomy: `c.slug = ANY(spelling)` wins,
and the one-level bucket walk runs only when the spelling is NOT a leaf of its own. A root
(`cafe` -> 79) and a word (`coffee` -> the cafe bucket) take the walk exactly as before.
Measured after: all 77 taxonomy slugs answer with exactly the count the corpus holds.

**Discipline note.** D505 was right that the filter must speak the product's vocabulary and
wrong about what that vocabulary IS: the reader it chose answers with the coarser fact, and
a hard filter must never be coarsened. The fix does not add a second reader - it keeps the
one reader and stops it from discarding what the caller wrote, then lets the plane that
owns the taxonomy arbitrate.

**Verified, not claimed.** The gate: **18 passed** - the planner keeps the caller's spelling
beside the bucket for the 12 measured leaves, the spelling is respelled by the ONE separator
rule, no spelling is invented when the caller named none, the SQL binds both slug sets, a
root still walks one tree level, and an unknown word still falls back to the bucket.
Proved to fail: dropping the spelling from the plan reddens **13** of the 18, and the live
check with it. Live contract re-measured on this database (**13 passed** in that file): six
leaves answer exactly their own count and three roots answer with their whole subtree.
Targeted regression (category, filter, search, intent, sql) -> **914 passed**; live (search
contract, preferences, sort preference, vocabulary spelling, conversation refinement) ->
**26 passed**; `mypy nexus_ai` -> **Success: no issues found in 59 source files**; `ruff
check .` -> **All checks passed**; eval gate -> **PASS - 2 suite(s), 0 failing**; the ten CI
checkers -> green.
## 519. D525 · the cuisine bridge named leaves no seed writes, and nothing read the seed to say so (`apps/ai/nexus_ai/nlu/lexicon.py`, `apps/ai/tests/test_the_cuisine_bridge_speaks_the_seeds_leaves.py`)

**What was measured.** `CUISINE_LEAVES` is the bridge between the word a user types
("japanese") and the leaf the taxonomy stores (`sushi`, `ramen`, `izakaya`), and its own
docstring makes a claim about a file in another plane: *"the leaves are the ones
`data/seed/seed_pools.py`'s `CAT_TREE` writes"*. Nothing read that file. A leaf the bridge
names and the taxonomy does not write is a leaf no merchant can carry, so the preference
fires on nothing - and a satisfied preference becomes the same as an unsatisfied one (D394),
which is the exact failure D522 measured from the other side. The seed writes 10 roots and
67 leaves; the bridge names 14 leaves across 12 cuisines. The counts happened to agree, but
they agreed by luck: the two planes are edited by hand, in different files, by different
units, and no gate held them to each other.

**The fix.** No product change - the invariant already held. The gap was the missing
reader. `apps/ai/tests/test_the_cuisine_bridge_speaks_the_seeds_leaves.py` imports the
seed's own `CAT_TREE` (the writer of the taxonomy the bridge names) and holds the bridge to
it in both directions: every leaf the bridge names is a leaf `CAT_TREE` writes, spelled the
seed's way; every cuisine the vocabulary names resolves to at least one real leaf; and the
bridge is not vacuously true - the taxonomy's own food leaves are still reachable through
it, so the mapping has not quietly emptied itself. The behavioural half pins the distinction
D394 depends on: a merchant carrying the leaf matches, and a merchant that merely sits in
the same ROOT does not, and neither does a merchant carrying a different leaf of that root.

**Discipline note.** This is the first gate in the project that reads the seed's taxonomy
from the AI lane's tests, and it is deliberately written against the counts it measured
(10 roots, 67 leaves) so that a re-seed which changes the taxonomy reddens the gate rather
than silently re-baselining it. The seed's `out/` and `out_smoke/` directories are not
tracked, so the gate reads `seed_pools.py` - the file that generates them - and not a
generated artefact.

**Verified, not claimed.** The gate: **37 passed** - 12 cuisines resolve to real leaves,
14 bridged leaves are all seed leaves, every nameable cuisine resolves, the bridge is not
vacuous, and 11 behavioural cases (leaf fires / root does not / sibling leaf does not).
Proved to fail, each probe put back and the file byte-compared afterwards: renaming one
bridged leaf to a slug the seed does not write -> **3 failed**; emptying one cuisine's
leaf tuple so it resolves to nothing -> **3 failed**; widening one cuisine to its whole
root -> **3 failed**. Targeted regression (cuisine, lexicon, vocabulary, canonical) ->
**1043 passed, 8 skipped**; `mypy nexus_ai` -> **Success: no issues found in 59 source
files**; `ruff check .` -> **All checks passed**; eval gate -> **PASS - 2 suite(s), 0
failing**; the ten CI checkers -> green.
## 520. D526 · a stored dislike that boosted the very thing it refused - "spicy" was a leaf nobody writes (`apps/ai/nexus_ai/nlu/lexicon.py`, `apps/ai/tests/test_the_spicy_word_speaks_the_seeds_own_leaves.py`, `apps/ai/tests/test_live_the_declared_dislike_demotes.py`)

**What was measured.** The seed writes the demo consumer's dislike as
`food/cuisine_dislike = {"values": ["spicy"]}`, and it writes each merchant's
`spicy_cuisine` attribute as `m["leaf"] in ("hotpot", "korean", "thai", "indian",
"malaysian", "sichuan", "hunan", "mexican")`. Two statements about one fact, and nothing
held them to each other. The preference reader resolved "spicy" through the cuisine bridge,
found no leaf of that name, and fell back to the identity - a leaf no merchant carries. The
dislike therefore answered the same number for every merchant. Measured on the live corpus,
over all 470 published merchants read as the demo user:

    the 54 merchants the corpus itself calls spicy -> mean 0.7403
    the other 416                                 -> mean 0.6591

A declared dislike that leaves the refused merchants **0.0812 above** the rest is the D522
inversion one plane over: the stored path instead of the transient one.

**The fix.** One bridge entry. `CUISINE_LEAVES["spicy"]` now carries the seed's own
derivation, respelled into the taxonomy that replaced it: `malaysian` is the seed's word
for the leaf the taxonomy now writes as `singmal`, and `sichuan`/`hunan`/`mexican` name
leaves the taxonomy does not write at all, so there is nothing to map them onto and they
drop out. Measured after: the 54 spicy merchants read **0.5532** against **0.6591** for
the rest - the dislike demotes. The same entry reaches the two other readers of the word
for free, because they already go through the bridge: a typed "辣"/"spicy" preference, and
the `avoid=["spicy"]` hard filter, both of which previously matched nothing.

**Discipline note.** The seed's derivation is the authority for what the word means, and
the taxonomy is the authority for how the leaves are spelled - so the gate reads the
derivation out of `data/seed/generate.py` with `ast` (not by importing a CLI with a
`main()`) and holds the bridge to it. The seed's own vocabulary is itself stale in the
same way - see the seed-lane item filed below - but "spicy" is the one case where the
derivation's intent is unambiguous and the respelling is mechanical, so it is fixed here
rather than reported.

**Verified, not claimed.** The gate: **9 passed** - the seed really declares the dislike,
the bridge carries the seed's own derivation respelled into the taxonomy, all 5 bridged
leaves match the word, a sibling leaf of the same root does not, and the stored dislike
separates the two merchants. Proved to fail four ways (each probe put back, file
byte-compared afterwards): the entry removed -> **8 failed**; narrowed to one leaf ->
**5 failed**; widened past the seed's derivation -> **1 failed**; left at the old dead
spelling `malaysian` -> **8 failed**. Live contract re-measured on this database
(**3 passed** in that file): the demo user's dislike row is on the plane, the corpus
carries the leaves, and the stored dislike scores the refused merchants below the rest.
Targeted regression (cuisine, lexicon, vocabulary, canonical, preference, spicy, avoid,
filter) -> **1418 passed, 24 skipped**; live (preferences, search contract, vocabulary
spelling, sort preference, canonical query, the new dislike gate) -> **30 passed**; `mypy
nexus_ai` -> **Success: no issues found in 59 source files**; `ruff check .` -> **All
checks passed**; eval gate -> **PASS - 2 suite(s), 0 failing**; the ten CI checkers ->
green.
## 521. D527 · a weak preference was evidence AGAINST the thing the user asked for (`apps/ai/nexus_ai/search/service.py`, `data/seed/generate.py`, `apps/ai/tests/test_a_weak_preference_is_not_evidence_against_it.py`, `apps/ai/tests/test_every_preference_the_seed_declares_is_read.py`, `apps/ai/tests/test_live_the_weak_preference_keeps_its_side.py`)

**What was measured.** Every boolean matcher in the ranker read its weight the same way -
`return w if v else (1.0 - w)` - which is only correct while `w > 0.5`. Below it the two
sides cross and the outcome the user asked for is scored BELOW the outcome they did not.
The seed declares `access/accessible` at **0.4**, the one row in the demo corpus under the
midpoint, so this was live, not hypothetical. Measured on this database over all 470
published merchants, with the seed's own row and the seed's own weight:

    the 267 merchants the corpus calls accessible -> mean 0.4000
    the 203 it calls inaccessible                 -> mean 0.6000

A user who said step-free access matters a little was served the merchants that have none
**0.2 above** the merchants that have it. The D522 inversion, one signal over, and invisible
for the same reason: every other weight in the corpus sits above 0.5.

Two more defects fell out of measuring it. The `style/outdoor` and `style/indoor` branch
read only the KEY and never the row's value, so `{"key": "outdoor", "value": false}` - a
refusal of the outdoors - was served as a request for it. And the `access/accessible` and
`access/mtr_near` matchers required **both** of their two attributes to be `False` before
they would call a merchant lacking the thing, while this corpus writes only one of the pair
- so 267 merchants answered True, 0 answered False, and the demoting half of the preference
was dead on arrival. The seed also declared its step-free row as `accessibility/step_free`,
a (kind, key) the ranker has no branch for at all: the row was dropped on the floor and the
user was told they had a preference that answered `None` for every merchant.

**The fix.** One helper, `_sided(w, liked=...)`: the distance from neutral carries the
strength and the side of neutral carries the sign, so a weight below 0.5 is weak evidence
FOR rather than evidence AGAINST. Every weight above 0.5 answers exactly what it answered
before (`w=0.9` still gives 0.9), so only the inverted half of the range moves. Measured
after: **0.6000** for the accessible merchants against **0.4000** for the rest. The
outdoor/indoor branch now reads the row's value; the two two-attribute matchers accept
either witness; the seed's row is respelled into the spelling the NLU itself emits; and the
`access/pet_friendly` branch, which was written twice in the same chain, is written once.

**Discipline note.** The seed's row was misspelled in a vocabulary the product does not use
anywhere else - the NLU's own `PREFERENCE_RULES` carries `("access", "accessible", ...)`,
and that is the spelling the matcher already had a branch for. So the row was respelled
rather than a second branch added for the same fact: one fact, one reader, one spelling.
The gate that holds it reads both planes with `ast` - the seed's `prefs` list and the
ranker's own `if kind == ... and key == ...` chain - so a new branch is picked up the moment
it is written, and a new misspelled row reddens the gate instead of landing silently.

**Verified, not claimed.** The ordering gate: **106 passed** - 12 boolean preferences x 7
weights across the whole range, the satisfying merchant always ahead, plus the strong-weight
regression guard (`w=0.9` still answers 0.9) and the refused direction (`value: false`). The
readability gate: **7 passed**. Live contract re-measured on this database (**2 passed**):
the corpus splits on the attribute on both sides, and the weak preference keeps the
accessible merchants ahead. Proved to fail: restoring `w if v else (1.0 - w)` reddens **24**
of the ordering checks; respelling the seed's row back to `accessibility/step_free`, or to
any kind the ranker has never heard of, reddens the readability check (each probe put back,
both files byte-compared afterwards). Targeted regression (preference, structured,
personalization, spicy, accessible, ambience, pet, mtr, scenic, budget, ranking, score) ->
**537 passed, 16 skipped**; live (preferences, search contract, dislike, weak preference,
vocabulary spelling, sort preference, canonical query, personalization signal) -> **33
passed, 1 skipped**; `mypy nexus_ai` -> **Success: no issues found in 59 source files**;
`ruff check .` -> **All checks passed**; eval gate -> **PASS - 2 suite(s), 0 failing**; the
CI checkers -> green.

## 522. D528 · a follow-up that changed its mind was dropped on the floor (`apps/ai/nexus_ai/nlu/state_merger.py`, `apps/ai/nexus_ai/search/service.py`, `apps/ai/tests/test_a_followup_can_change_its_mind.py`, `apps/ai/tests/test_live_conversation_refinement.py`)

**What was measured.** `_absorb` pulls whatever a follow-up resolved into the carried
state, and its preference half tested `if p["key"] not in {the keys the state holds}`.
A preference the state already carried was therefore DROPPED - and dropping it is not
neutral:

    我想要海景  then  唔好海景  ->  view=scenic, polarity **+1**

The negation the user typed in the follow-up was discarded and the thing they refused
stayed a LIKE, which the ranking lane then boosts: the D523 inversion, reached from the
merge lane instead of the polarity lane. And the same test dropped a plain change of
mind:

    我想食日本菜  then  想食泰國菜  ->  cuisine=japanese, and `changes: []`

The user was answered with the cuisine they had abandoned, and because nothing was
recorded no `agent_run` could explain what the turn did (§34: every change is
recorded). Measured on the live plane, through the stream the product answers on: the
first turn's cards carried `符合你這次的要求：japanese` and the follow-up's carried the
same string - the user's second sentence had moved nothing at all.

**The fix.** The turn's values for a key REPLACE the state's values for that key, and
the replacement is recorded with the polarity attached, so a flip from +1 to -1 is
visible in the record and not only in the state. Re-stating what the state already
carries is still a no-op, and a new key still merges without disturbing the others.
Measured live after: the follow-up's cards carry `符合你這次的要求：thai`, the state
carries `("cuisine", "thai")` and no longer `("cuisine", "japanese")`, and
`唔好海景` leaves `view=scenic` at polarity **-1**.

**A second reader of the same weight.** `make_occasion_match` was the one matcher of
fifteen that never read its weight at all - it answered a hardcoded `1.0` / `0.0` - so
an occasion the user cares about a little swung the personalization signal over its
whole range and one they care about a great deal swung it no further. It now answers
through `_sided(w, ...)` (D527) like every other boolean matcher, and an attribute the
corpus does not declare is still neutral at 0.5.

**Verified, not claimed.** The merge gate `test_a_followup_can_change_its_mind.py`:
**7 passed** - a different cuisine lands, the replacement is recorded, a negation typed
in the follow-up flips the polarity, the flip is visible in the record, a re-stated
preference is a no-op, a new key does not disturb the others, and the merge stays pure.
The ordering gate `test_a_weak_preference_is_not_evidence_against_it.py`, extended with
the five occasion rows: **146 passed**. The live gate
`test_live_conversation_refinement.py`: **4 passed** - the two-turn refinement in both
spellings still works, and the two measurements above are taken off the live stream.
Proved to fail: making the occasion matcher ignore its weight reddens **5** of the
ordering checks; restoring the membership test reddens **4** of the merge checks and
**2** of the live ones (each probe put back, the files byte-compared afterwards).
Targeted regression (`-k "merge or refinement or state or conversation or nlu or
understand or intent"`) -> **342 passed, 13 skipped**; (`-k "preference or structured
or occasion or personaliz or merge or refinement or state"`) -> **533 passed, 18
skipped**; `mypy nexus_ai` -> **Success: no issues found in 59 source files**;
`ruff check .` -> **All checks passed**; eval gate -> **PASS - 2 suite(s), 0 failing**.

## 523. D529 · a refusal was evidence FOR everything else, at full strength (`apps/ai/nexus_ai/search/service.py`, `apps/ai/tests/test_the_intent_cuisine_reads_the_rows_columns.py`, `apps/ai/tests/test_a_refusal_is_not_evidence_for_everything_else.py`, `apps/ai/tests/test_live_the_refusal_does_not_flatten_the_lane.py`)

**What was measured.** The transient path - the one that serves the preferences the user
typed in THIS query - answered a cuisine preference it could not match with the side of
neutral the user was NOT on:

    a cuisine the user LIKED    -> 0.5   (no evidence either way)
    a cuisine the user DISLIKED -> 1.0   (the maximum)

"The merchant is not the refused cuisine, therefore a perfect match." It is not a match.
The merchant simply is not the thing the user turned down, and the user said nothing
about how well it fits them. Answering the maximum there made a refusal evidence FOR
everything else at full strength - and because the aggregation across preferences is a
maximum (D397), one typed refusal erased every other preference the user had. Measured
on this database (470 published merchants), a declared `quiet` at weight 0.9 plus a typed
refusal of Japanese:

    before:  the 188 quiet merchants  -> 0.9000
             the 282 loud merchants   -> 1.0000
    after:   the 188 quiet merchants  -> 0.9000
             the 282 loud merchants   -> 0.5000

Before the fix the personalization lane was FLAT: 470 merchants, one value, and the
preference the user had declared had no effect on the order they were served in. This
is the D527 shape once more - a signal answering a question it was not asked - reached
from the transient path instead of the stored one, and it is the residue D522 left
behind: the `1.0` was the symptom of a match that never fired, and when the match was
repaired the answer was pinned as though it had been the design.

**The fix.** The non-match answers neutral, in both directions, exactly as a LIKE
already did. The refused cuisine is still demoted to 0.0 - refusing something still
excludes it. What changed is that refusing something no longer promotes everything
else. The row that pinned the old behaviour in the D522 gate was rewritten with the
measurement that overturns it, so the two units do not disagree about the same line.

**Verified, not claimed.** `test_a_refusal_is_not_evidence_for_everything_else.py`:
**6 passed** - the refused cuisine still demotes to the floor, a liked cuisine still
boosts, a refusal no longer promotes what it did not name, the lane can still tell the
two halves apart, a declared preference survives a refusal typed in the same turn, and
the lane is unchanged when nobody refuses anything. Live
(`test_live_the_refusal_does_not_flatten_the_lane.py`): **4 passed** - the corpus splits
on both sides, the refusal does not lift the half the user did not name above the half
it did, the declared 0.9 survives, and the lane is not flat. Proved to fail: restoring
`0.5 if polarity > 0 else 1.0` reddens **5** of the fourteen checks (the probe put back,
the file byte-compared afterwards). Targeted regression (`-k "preference or structured
or occasion or personaliz or merge or refinement or state or polarity or cuisine or
transient or ranking"`) -> **803 passed, 24 skipped**; (`-k "search or rank or card or
score or facet or filter or avoid"`) -> **818 passed, 26 skipped**; `mypy nexus_ai` ->
**Success: no issues found in 59 source files**; `ruff check .` -> **All checks
passed**; eval gate -> **PASS - 2 suite(s), 0 failing**.

## 524. D530 · the preference the user TYPES read an attribute no corpus writes (`apps/ai/nexus_ai/search/service.py`, `apps/ai/tests/test_a_followup_can_change_its_mind.py`, `apps/ai/tests/test_a_typed_preference_reaches_the_attribute_the_corpus_writes.py`, `apps/ai/tests/test_the_typed_preference_speaks_the_corpus_spelling.py`, `apps/ai/tests/test_live_the_typed_preference_moves_the_lane.py`)

**What was measured.** The ranker answers the same question twice: once for a preference
the user DECLARED, out of `user_preferences` - a long `if kind == ... and key == ...`
chain that names each attribute explicitly - and once for a preference the user typed in
THIS query, out of the Intent, which derives the attribute name from the (kind, key)
pair (`date_occasion` from `occasion/date`). Nineteen of the twenty rows in the
lexicon's `PREFERENCE_RULES` resolve through one of those two spellings to an attribute
the seed writes. One does not. `time_pref/open_late` derives `open_late_time_pref` and
`time_pref_open_late`; the seed, the stored branch and the corpus all spell it
`opens_late`. Measured on this database:

    the corpus splits 266 merchants that open late / 204 that do not
    the stored path scores those halves          0.9 / 0.1
    the typed path, before the fix, scored       0 of 470 merchants

A user who typed a late-night request got a personalization lane that moved nothing at
all, and nothing on any surface said so. This is the D518 shape (one fact, two readers,
and the copy serving the live query is the broken one) reached a third time, and the
D522 shape (a reader looking where the fact is not written) reached from the attribute
side rather than the JSONB side.

**The fix.** `_INTENT_ATTR_ALIASES` carries the one (kind, key) whose attribute is not
spellable from the pair, naming the spelling the stored branch already reads - one fact,
one reader, one spelling (D527). Measured live after: the 266 late merchants answer 1.0
and the 204 that close early answer 0.0.

**A defect the gate found in this lane's own work.** `test_vocabulary_is_the_reference`
reddened on D528's fixture: it had typed a CJK code point (U+65B8) the product's
vocabulary does not carry - D520's defect, in a file written two units later, caught by
the gate that was written for it. The fixture now takes its word from the lexicon's own
`ambience/quiet` row, as D409 requires.

**Verified, not claimed.**
`test_a_typed_preference_reaches_the_attribute_the_corpus_writes.py`: **4 passed** - the
typed preference reaches the merchant that stays open, demotes the one that closes, the
two halves are separated, and the declared and the typed preference read the same
